Luteinizing hormone: a signal from the anterior pituitary that stimulates testosterone release in testes and helps trigger egg release and formation of temporary hormone-producing tissue in ovaries.

frames.title: Gametes and chromosome sets
frames.scenario: A primary spermatocyte has completed DNA replication. Count human chromosome sets, chromosomes and DNA molecules before meiosis I and in one product after meiosis I.
orderedExplanation: Begin with two homologous sets and 46 chromosomes.
Replication creates two chromatids per chromosome: 92 DNA molecules, still two sets.
Meiosis I separates homologues: each product has one set, 23 chromosomes and 46 DNA molecules.
frames.conclusion: Before meiosis I: 2 sets, 46 chromosomes, 92 DNA molecules. After meiosis I, per cell: 1 set, 23 chromosomes, 46 DNA molecules.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Division and differentiation
frames.scenario: One typical primary spermatocyte completes both meiotic divisions. Predict the immediate products and explain why they still need further change.
orderedExplanation: Meiosis I produces two secondary spermatocytes with duplicated chromosomes.
Meiosis II separates sister chromatids, producing four haploid spermatids.
Differentiation reshapes each spermatid, including its acrosome, compact nucleus and flagellum.
frames.conclusion: The immediate products are four haploid spermatids. Meiosis establishes their chromosome content; differentiation and later maturation support the form and functions associated with sperm.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Hormone sources and targets
frames.scenario: In a simplified pathway, GnRH stimulates the anterior pituitary, which releases LH. Identify the next target and response, then contrast the FSH branch.

frames.conclusion: LH acts on interstitial cells to support testosterone production. FSH acts through Sertoli cells to support germ-cell development. The branches interact but do not have identical targets.

frames.title: Two coordinated cycles
frames.scenario: Place follicle development, ovulation, corpus-luteum function, endometrial rebuilding and secretory maintenance on two aligned tracks in a typical simplified cycle.
orderedExplanation: Use an ovarian track for follicular phase → ovulation → luteal phase.
Use a uterine track for shedding → rebuilding → secretory maintenance.
Align the tracks by changing hormone signals, rather than calling a uterine event an ovarian structure.
frames.conclusion: Follicular estrogen supports rebuilding; luteal progesterone supports a secretory endometrium. These coordinated tracks have different events and should remain separately labelled.

frames.title: Follicle growth and changing feedback
frames.scenario: In the supplied series, estrogen's relative index rises to 10 on day 12 and LH peaks at 18 on day 14. Explain a plausible connection and one limitation of these data.
orderedExplanation: Find day 12 on the time axis. Read the estrogen index as 10 on its own relative scale.
Find day 14 and read the LH peak as 18 on the LH scale. The LH peak comes after the estrogen rise. Do not compare 18 with 10 as if they were amounts on a shared concentration scale.
Connect the order to the mechanism: sustained high estrogen near ovulation can increase upstream activity through positive feedback, helping produce an LH surge.
State the limit: the sample points are two days apart, and other conditions were not measured. The pattern supports the connection but does not prove an exact trigger level or hour of ovulation.
frames.conclusion: The pattern is consistent with an estrogen-associated feedback transition preceding an LH surge. The sampled indices do not by themselves prove a universal threshold or the exact hour of ovulation.

frames.title: Corpus luteum and the endometrium
frames.scenario: In a cycle without an ongoing pregnancy signal, corpus-luteum function declines. Predict the effect on progesterone support and the endometrium.
orderedExplanation: Identify the corpus luteum as an important post-ovulation progesterone source.
Follow reduced luteal function to declining hormone support.
Connect withdrawal of support with endometrial breakdown and shedding in the model.
frames.conclusion: Progesterone support declines, and the maintained endometrium breaks down. The oocyte itself is not the source of the shed uterine tissue.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Graphs and cycle variation
frames.scenario: Plot the supplied progesterone indices at days 2, 7, 12, 14, 21 and 28: 1, 1, 1, 2, 10 and 1. Identify the highest sampled value and a limit on timing.
orderedExplanation: Put day on the horizontal axis and progesterone relative index on the vertical axis.
Plot all six points with a legend if other hormones are added.
Identify day 21 as the highest sampled value, while leaving the intervals between samples uncertain.
frames.conclusion: The highest sampled progesterone index is 10 on day 21. This does not establish that the true peak occurred exactly on day 21 or that its concentration exceeds another hormone measured on a different relative scale.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Hormonal technologies and perspectives
frames.scenario: A fictional classroom source describes a technology that supplies hormone signals which reduce the upstream drive for follicle maturation and ovulation. Explain the mechanism and name evidence needed to evaluate a public-information claim.
orderedExplanation: Trace added signals to hypothalamic/pituitary feedback in the stated model.
Connect reduced upstream drive with altered ovarian events, without assuming all technologies use the same mechanism.
Separate biological effectiveness evidence from questions of access, privacy, environmental impact, cultural acceptability and cost.
frames.conclusion: The mechanism is consistent with suppression of ovulatory signalling in the supplied model. Evaluating the claim also needs a defined outcome, comparison group, time interval and transparent account of uncertainty and user perspectives.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

checkpoint.prompt: Can separate relative hormone indices be added as a total blood concentration?
checkpoint.comparisonGuide: No. Their separate reference scales do not provide compatible concentration units.

framing.observableQuestion: Why does successful fertilization not guarantee implantation?
framing.learningGoal: Sequence gamete interaction, restoration of diploidy, cleavage, blastocyst formation and implantation, including a bounded IVF comparison.
framing.priorKnowledgeSupport: Gametes contain one chromosome set. The uterine tube and endometrium are different locations. Cell number, total size and developmental organization describe different changes.

retrieval.prompt: Put fertilization, cleavage, blastocyst formation and implantation in order.
retrieval.comparisonGuide: Fertilization → cleavage → blastocyst formation → implantation in a suitable endometrium.

evidenceSlip.prompt: Locate one IVF step in the developmental sequence and explain an outcome it supports without guaranteeing the next step.
criteria: Distinguish its measured outcome from a later outcome.

frames.title: Gametes meet
frames.scenario: An oocyte and sperm are present in a fictional uterine-tube model, but the sperm cannot complete the interactions needed to pass the oocyte's coverings and fuse with its membrane. Has fertilization been demonstrated?
orderedExplanation: Distinguish shared location from successful cellular interaction.
Identify passage through surrounding coverings and membrane fusion as necessary events in the model.
Seek evidence of activation and combining parental genetic contributions before calling the sequence complete.
frames.conclusion: No. The presence of both gametes in the same region is insufficient. The failed interaction interrupts the sequence before the full fertilization process is established.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Combining chromosome sets
frames.scenario: A normal human sperm contributes 23 chromosomes and the female gamete contributes 23. A hypothetical error allows a second complete sperm contribution. Compare the set totals without predicting an individual outcome.
orderedExplanation: One paternal set plus one maternal set restores two sets: 46 chromosomes.
A second paternal set would add another 23 in this simplified counting model.
Distinguish the resulting three-set count from a normal diploid fertilization.
frames.conclusion: The normal combination is 2n = 46. The hypothetical additional complete contribution gives three sets, 69 chromosomes, showing why mechanisms restricting extra sperm entry matter.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Cleavage and blastocyst formation
frames.scenario: A simplified embryo changes from one cell to two, four and eight while its overall outer size remains similar. What changed, and what did not follow from the observation?
orderedExplanation: Count cells at each stage.
Recognize cleavage as repeated divisions distributing the original material into smaller cells.
Separate increased cell number from an increase in the embryo's total external size.
frames.conclusion: Cell number increased through cleavage. The observation does not show proportional overall growth. Later blastocyst formation includes organization of an outer layer, inner cell mass and fluid-filled cavity.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Implantation and reproductive technology
frames.scenario: A fictional IVF sequence includes oocyte retrieval, fertilization in a laboratory, early development and embryo transfer. A report states that transfer guarantees implantation. Correct it.
orderedExplanation: Place laboratory fertilization before early embryo development.
Place embryo transfer before possible attachment and interaction with a suitable endometrium.
Keep successful transfer, implantation and continuing development as different outcomes.
frames.conclusion: Transfer places an embryo in the uterus; it does not guarantee implantation or continuing pregnancy. Each outcome needs its own definition and evidence.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

checkpoint.prompt: Does embryo transfer itself establish that implantation occurred?
checkpoint.comparisonGuide: No. Transfer precedes possible implantation; each needs separate evidence.

framing.observableQuestion: How does early development maintain support while establishing new tissues?

framing.priorKnowledgeSupport: Hormone action depends on a source and a responsive target. Cleavage increases cell number. Tissues with a shared adult function can have different embryonic origins.

retrieval.prompt: Give the early hCG support chain in order.
retrieval.comparisonGuide: Trophoblast-related hCG → maintained corpus luteum → progesterone support → maintained endometrium.

evidenceSlip.prompt: Correct one overgeneralized germ-layer claim using a named tissue example and one qualification.
criteria: Distinguish a specific tissue from a mixed organ or functional category.

frames.title: A signal maintains the early pregnancy
frames.scenario: In an early-pregnancy model, trophoblast-related tissue releases hCG. Trace the connection to endometrial support without placing hCG production in the ovary.
orderedExplanation: Identify the developing trophoblast-related source of hCG.
Trace its action to maintenance of corpus-luteum function.
Connect luteal progesterone support with maintenance of the endometrium during this early interval.
frames.conclusion: The chain is trophoblast-related hCG → maintained corpus luteum → progesterone support → maintained endometrium. Later placental hormone production changes the relative roles of these sources.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Gastrulation establishes layers
frames.scenario: A diagram shows cells reorganizing into ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm. Another shows one cell becoming two without that three-layer arrangement. Name the processes and their key difference.
orderedExplanation: Use rising cell number to identify the cleavage example.
Use coordinated cell movement and three-layer organization to identify gastrulation.
Connect the new spatial arrangement with later tissue-development pathways.
frames.conclusion: Cleavage increases cell number through division. Gastrulation establishes the three primary germ layers through organized developmental changes; it is not merely another name for any cell division.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Layer-to-tissue relationships
frames.scenario: Classify nervous tissue, skeletal muscle and the epithelial lining of much of the digestive tract by their usual primary germ-layer relationships. Then explain why “all endocrine glands are endoderm” fails.
orderedExplanation: Match nervous tissue with ectoderm, skeletal muscle with mesoderm and much digestive epithelium with endoderm.
Recognize that an organ can contain tissues with different origins.
Compare endocrine examples: pituitary tissues relate to ectoderm, adrenal cortex to mesoderm, and pancreatic endocrine tissue to endoderm.
frames.conclusion: The three named tissues match ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm respectively. Endocrine function does not imply one universal developmental origin.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Developmental evidence
frames.scenario: Two fictional timelines label an event “week 6,” but one counts from fertilization and the other from the last menstrual period. Can the entries be aligned directly?
orderedExplanation: Read the time origin in each legend.
Recognize that gestational dating commonly starts about two weeks before fertilization in a simplified typical cycle.
Convert only with that explicit approximation and retain biological timing variation.
frames.conclusion: The entries cannot be aligned as identical ages without conversion. In the simplified convention, six weeks after fertilization is about eight gestational weeks; this is an approximate relationship, not an exact date for every pregnancy.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

checkpoint.prompt: Does endocrine function mean every gland develops from endoderm?
checkpoint.comparisonGuide: No. Endocrine tissues have several origins; function does not define one germ layer.

framing.observableQuestion: How can separate maternal and fetal circulations exchange materials?

framing.priorKnowledgeSupport: A membrane can separate compartments while allowing some substances to move. Artery and vein names describe flow direction. Comparisons need counts, denominators and a stated time origin.

retrieval.prompt: Name the umbilical vessel carrying blood toward the fetus and explain why the circulations remain distinct.
retrieval.comparisonGuide: The umbilical vein carries blood toward the fetus; exchange occurs across tissues between separate blood compartments.

evidenceSlip.prompt: Use the early/later exposure data to state a comparison, its denominator and one causal or individual-prediction limit.
criteria: Name the interval and sample size.
Retain a design or prediction limit.

frames.title: Support membranes
frames.scenario: Match four structures to distinct roles in a human developmental model: amnion, chorion, yolk sac and allantois. Avoid importing the large food-yolk model of a bird egg unchanged.
orderedExplanation: Connect the amnion with the fluid-filled protective environment.
Connect chorionic tissue with the fetal contribution to placental structures and exchange relationships.
Describe early yolk-sac and allantoic contributions in human development without calling them a large stored-yolk meal or a waste-storage sac for the whole pregnancy.
frames.conclusion: The amnion surrounds the fluid environment; the chorion contributes to placental relationships. The human yolk sac has early developmental roles including blood formation, while allantoic development relates to structures associated with the connecting region and urinary development.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Maternal and fetal circulation
frames.scenario: Trace oxygen from maternal blood to fetal blood at the placenta, then to the fetus. Include the direction of the umbilical vein and arteries.
orderedExplanation: Keep maternal blood and fetal capillaries as separate compartments divided by exchange tissues.
Show oxygen moving across that interface into fetal blood.
Trace the umbilical vein toward the fetus and the umbilical arteries back toward the placenta.
frames.conclusion: Oxygen crosses an exchange interface rather than normally requiring bulk mixing of the two circulations. The umbilical vein carries blood toward the fetus; the arteries carry it away from the fetus toward the placenta.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Organ formation across development
frames.scenario: Place cleavage, gastrulation and early organ-system formation in order, then explain why the end of early organogenesis does not mean that every organ is fully mature.
orderedExplanation: Begin with cleavage and early cell organization.
Follow with gastrulation and establishment of germ-layer relationships.
Place early organ formation after these foundations while retaining later growth and functional maturation.
frames.conclusion: The order is cleavage → gastrulation → early organ-system formation. Development continues through later growth and maturation; some systems also undergo major changes around birth and afterward.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Environmental influence and evidence
frames.scenario: In the supplied non-human cell model, an early interval has marker M in 4 out of 40 control samples and 20 out of 40 exposed samples. A later interval has 5/40 and 9/40. Compare the exposed-minus-control proportions.
orderedExplanation: Calculate early proportions: 0.10 and 0.50, giving a difference of 0.40.
Calculate later proportions: 0.125 and 0.225, giving a difference of 0.10.
Compare the differences while checking whether the groups and exposure conditions are otherwise comparable.
frames.conclusion: The difference is 40 percentage points early and 10 percentage points later. The supplied data suggest a stronger association in the early interval, but they do not predict an individual's outcome or prove all other causes were controlled.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

checkpoint.prompt: Does separate blood circulation mean that no substance can cross the placenta?
checkpoint.comparisonGuide: No. Exchange occurs across the interface without normal bulk blood mixing.

framing.observableQuestion: How do feedback, birth and feeding establish a new support system?
framing.learningGoal: Explain labour feedback and newborn transitions, distinguish milk synthesis from ejection and evaluate a bounded technology claim.
framing.priorKnowledgeSupport: A feedback loop has an initiating stimulus and a response. Production and transport are distinct functions. A technology acts on particular steps and must be evaluated against a defined outcome.

retrieval.prompt: Match prolactin and oxytocin to the two lactation functions.
retrieval.comparisonGuide: Prolactin supports milk synthesis; oxytocin supports ejection through contraction of surrounding cells.

evidenceSlip.prompt: Revise one claim about birth, lactation or reproductive technology using a mechanism, evidence and a stated limit.

frames.title: Labour and positive feedback
frames.scenario: Complete a simplified labour loop starting with cervical stretch. Identify why the loop does not continue indefinitely after delivery.
orderedExplanation: Cervical stretch provides sensory input associated with oxytocin release from the posterior pituitary.
Oxytocin supports uterine contractions, which can increase stretch during labour.
Delivery removes the major stretch stimulus sustaining this particular loop.
frames.conclusion: The response reinforces the initiating change during the process. Removing the stimulus interrupts the loop; positive feedback does not mean unlimited activity without conditions.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Birth and the transition
frames.scenario: Sequence cervical dilation, delivery of the baby and delivery of the placenta in a simplified account. Relate the newborn's support transition to breathing and circulation.
orderedExplanation: Place dilation before passage through the birth canal in the typical sequence.
Place placental delivery after birth of the baby.
Connect the start of effective lung gas exchange with circulatory changes rather than treating placental support as unchanged after separation.
frames.conclusion: The simplified sequence is dilation → birth → placental delivery. Breathing and circulatory transition establish a different gas-exchange arrangement from fetal placental support.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Milk synthesis and release
frames.scenario: In a simplified lactation case, milk is present in secretory tissue but little reaches the outlet during a test of the release response. Which pathway should the model examine first?
orderedExplanation: Separate synthesis by milk-producing cells from movement of existing milk.
Connect prolactin mainly with milk synthesis and oxytocin with contraction of surrounding myoepithelial cells.
Examine the release pathway while retaining transport and other conditions as alternatives.
frames.conclusion: The immediate observation directs attention to milk ejection and movement, including the oxytocin-linked response. It does not by itself prove that milk synthesis is absent.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Technologies, infertility and perspectives
frames.scenario: A fictional report compares a treatment aimed at ovulatory signalling with a procedure that bypasses a transport step. Both are advertised as “fixing infertility.” Explain why the comparison needs more detail.
orderedExplanation: Locate the proposed interruption in each case: signalling or transport.
Match each technology to the step it is designed to influence.
Define the measured outcome and compare uncertainty, access, cultural and ethical concerns, environmental resource use and cost.
frames.conclusion: The technologies address different mechanisms and may be relevant to different circumstances. A broad shared label does not establish equal effectiveness, suitability or consequences.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Investigating and communicating a claim
frames.scenario: A peer reads the developmental dataset and says, “Every early exposure causes an effect, while later exposure is harmless.” Use the supplied counts to revise both claims.
orderedExplanation: In the early exposed group, 20 of 40 have the recorded outcome, so the observation is not universal.
In the later exposed group, 9 of 40 have the outcome compared with 5 of 40 controls, so harmlessness is not established.
Compare the groups and acknowledge design limits before proposing a follow-up.
frames.conclusion: The supplied data show a larger exposed-control difference early, not an effect in every early case or zero association later. A follow-up should control relevant conditions, define the outcome and improve replication without exposing people to harm.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

checkpoint.prompt: What interrupts the cervical-stretch feedback loop after delivery?
checkpoint.comparisonGuide: Delivery removes the major stretch stimulus sustaining that particular loop.

framing.observableQuestion: How can a cell double its DNA without doubling its chromosome sets?
framing.learningGoal: Distinguish packaging, genes, chromosomes, homologous sets and sister copies, and interpret a karyotype within its resolution.
framing.priorKnowledgeSupport: Cells store hereditary information in DNA. A copy and a set are different counting units. An image shows features only at its own scale and in its sampled material.

retrieval.prompt: For 2n = 4 after replication, give chromosomes, DNA molecules and sets.
retrieval.comparisonGuide: Four chromosomes, eight DNA molecules and two homologous sets.

evidenceSlip.prompt: Use a chromosome drawing or karyotype to support one count or structural claim and state a limit on what the image reveals.
criteria: State a resolution or sampling limit.

frames.title: DNA packaging
frames.scenario: A drawing labels a whole chromosome “one gene” and a short DNA region “one chromosome.” Repair the hierarchy.
orderedExplanation: Start with DNA wrapped around associated proteins as chromatin.
Identify a chromosome as one organized DNA molecule with its associated proteins at an unreplicated stage.
Place many gene regions along that DNA rather than equating one region with the whole chromosome.
frames.conclusion: A gene is a region of DNA; a chromosome contains a much longer DNA molecule and many such regions. Packaging changes visibility without creating new genes by itself.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Sets and copies
frames.scenario: A model cell has 2n = 4. Count sets, chromosomes and DNA molecules before replication and just after replication.
orderedExplanation: Before replication, identify two sets containing two chromosome types each.
Count four unreplicated chromosomes and four DNA molecules.
After replication, keep four chromosomes but count eight sister-chromatid DNA molecules.
frames.conclusion: Before replication: two sets, four chromosomes, four DNA molecules. After replication: two sets, four chromosomes, eight DNA molecules.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Reading karyotypes
frames.scenario: A fictional karyotype contains three copies of one chromosome type and two copies of each remaining autosomal type. What can the image support, and what remains unmeasured?
orderedExplanation: Use the supplied size and banding key to identify the chromosome types.
Count the copies of each type rather than grouping by colour alone.
Report the observed extra copy without inferring a complete sequence or every future trait.
frames.conclusion: The image supports an extra copy of the identified chromosome type in the sampled cell. It does not reveal every DNA variant, all tissues in the organism or a complete developmental outcome.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

checkpoint.prompt: Does an X-shaped chromosome represent two homologues?
checkpoint.comparisonGuide: No. It is one replicated chromosome with joined sister chromatids.

framing.observableQuestion: What can a snapshot of cells reveal about a process unfolding over time?

framing.priorKnowledgeSupport: Replication produces sister copies. A proportion is a part divided by a whole. A snapshot count and a direct time measurement are different kinds of evidence.

retrieval.prompt: What changes during S phase, and what remains unchanged before division?

evidenceSlip.prompt: Use the supplied 72/100 interphase count to give a 20-hour-model estimate and one assumption that limits it.

frames.title: Interphase
frames.scenario: For a model cell with 2n = 6, compare G1, the end of S phase and G2.

During S phase, DNA is copied without separating sister centromeres.
At the end of S phase and in G2, record six duplicated chromosomes and twelve DNA molecules.

frames.title: Control and division

framing.observableQuestion: How do duplicated chromosomes reach two daughter nuclei?
framing.learningGoal: Sequence chromosome changes, explain counting during anaphase and classify authentic cell images from visible features.
framing.priorKnowledgeSupport: A duplicated chromosome has sister copies. A whole cell and one pole are different counting boundaries. Plant and animal cells form division boundaries differently.

retrieval.prompt: In mitotic anaphase from 2n = 4, count chromosomes in the whole cell and at one pole.
retrieval.comparisonGuide: Eight across the still-undivided cell; four at each pole and in each resulting daughter nucleus.

evidenceSlip.prompt: Assign one authentic image to a stage using a visible feature and record any uncertainty in the view.

frames.title: Preparing to separate
frames.scenario: A cell image shows condensed chromosomes, and a later image shows chromosomes arranged near the equatorial plane with spindle attachments. Sequence the observations.
orderedExplanation: Use condensation as evidence consistent with prophase progression.
Use equatorial chromosome alignment and appropriate attachments as evidence of metaphase.
Keep observations about visible structures separate from details too small to resolve in the image.
frames.conclusion: The condensation stage precedes the aligned metaphase arrangement. Stage identification should be justified from the visible structures, not merely a memorized picture position.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Separating copies
frames.scenario: A 2n = 4 model cell reaches mitotic anaphase. Count chromosomes in the still-undivided cell and at each pole.
orderedExplanation: Before separation, the cell has four duplicated chromosomes.
When sister centromeres separate, each former chromatid is counted as a chromosome.
Count eight chromosomes across the whole cell, with four moving toward each pole.
frames.conclusion: The whole anaphase cell temporarily contains eight chromosomes by this counting convention; each future daughter nucleus receives four. This is not evidence that each daughter becomes tetraploid.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Finishing cell division
frames.scenario: Compare how a typical animal cell and a typical plant cell divide their cytoplasm after nuclear division.
orderedExplanation: In the animal model, trace constriction of a cleavage furrow.
In the plant model, trace cell-plate formation and development of the separating boundary.
Keep these cytokinesis mechanisms distinct from chromosome separation during mitosis.
frames.conclusion: Both mechanisms partition cytoplasm into daughter cells, but they form the separating boundary differently. Mitosis and cytokinesis are related processes with distinct events.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Observation and simulation
frames.scenario: Use the authentic prepared-cell images assigned to this activity. For each proposed stage, name one visible feature before comparing with the supplied stage key.
orderedExplanation: Inspect the actual image for diffuse or condensed nuclear material and chromosome arrangement.
Record the observed feature before selecting a stage label.
Compare the label with the guide and revise any assignment whose supporting feature is absent or unclear.
frames.conclusion: A defensible answer pairs each stage with image evidence. The supplied synthetic 100-cell table is a separate calculation dataset and must not be described as a count made from these five images.

checkpoint.prompt: Does chromosome condensation alone establish metaphase?

framing.observableQuestion: Which separation event reduces chromosome sets?
framing.learningGoal: Trace homolog pairing, exchange and two meiotic divisions, comparing them with mitosis using explicit counts.
framing.priorKnowledgeSupport: Homologues carry corresponding loci; sisters are replicated copies. Ploidy counts homologous sets. DNA replicates before the two-division meiotic sequence.

retrieval.prompt: Name what separates in meiosis I and meiosis II.
retrieval.comparisonGuide: Meiosis I separates homologues; meiosis II separates sister copies without another S phase.

evidenceSlip.prompt: Follow a 2n = 4 model through both divisions and explain where reduction occurs.
criteria: Keep sister separation and DNA-copy changes distinct.

frames.title: Pairing and exchange
frames.scenario: In a 2n = 4 model, one homologous pair carries A and a. Show crossing over between nonsister chromatids without exchanging an entire chromosome set.
orderedExplanation: Replicate each homologue before pairing.
Pair corresponding homologues and select one chromatid from each for an exchange at matching regions.
Track the exchanged segments while preserving chromosome number and the overall homologous pair.
frames.conclusion: Crossing over can create new allele combinations along chromatids. It exchanges corresponding DNA regions between nonsister chromatids rather than creating extra sets.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: First meiotic division
frames.scenario: A replicated 2n = 4 cell completes meiosis I. Count chromosomes and sets in one daughter cell and name what separated.
orderedExplanation: Start with two homologous pairs, each chromosome duplicated.
Separate the homologues of each pair while sister chromatids remain joined.
Count two duplicated chromosomes in each product, representing one complete set.
frames.conclusion: Each product is haploid, n = 2, with two duplicated chromosomes and four DNA molecules. Homologues, not sister chromatids, separated in this division.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Second meiotic division
frames.scenario: Each product of meiosis I in a 2n = 4 model has two duplicated chromosomes. Describe meiosis II and the final per-cell counts.
orderedExplanation: Begin without another S phase.
Separate sister chromatids in each of the two cells.
Partition the separated chromosomes into four final products, each with one set.
frames.conclusion: Each final product has n = 2: two unduplicated chromosomes and two DNA molecules. Meiosis II separates copies without another reduction in homologous-set number.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Comparing divisions
frames.scenario: Compare mitosis and meiosis for a replicated 2n = 4 starting cell, using products and separation events.
orderedExplanation: Mitosis separates sister copies in one division and normally produces two diploid daughters.
Meiosis I separates homologues and meiosis II separates sister copies.
Count four haploid products after the full meiotic sequence, while retaining the simplified successful-division assumptions.
frames.conclusion: Mitosis normally preserves set number in two products; meiosis reduces it in four products after two divisions. Replication precedes both sequences but occurs only once before the two meiotic divisions.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

checkpoint.prompt: Is another DNA-replication phase normally inserted between meiosis I and II?
checkpoint.comparisonGuide: No. One replication precedes the two divisions.

framing.observableQuestion: How can variation and chromosome errors arise from the same division sequence?
framing.learningGoal: Compare gamete development, sources of combinations, error timings and twin origins with bounded developmental claims.
framing.priorKnowledgeSupport: Meiosis I separates homologues and meiosis II separates sisters. Gamete content, cytoplasmic size and developmental timing are different features. Fertilization combines two contributions.

retrieval.prompt: Compare the simple meiosis-I and one-cell meiosis-II nondisjunction gamete patterns.
retrieval.comparisonGuide: Meiosis I: two n+1 and two n−1. The stated meiosis-II error: two normal, one n+1 and one n−1.

evidenceSlip.prompt: Use one variation or nondisjunction model to trace an event to its products, including a boundary on the prediction.
criteria: Follow the affected chromosomes or combinations.

frames.title: Gamete development
frames.scenario: Compare a typical spermatocyte lineage with a typical human oocyte lineage in chromosome reduction and cytoplasmic allocation.
orderedExplanation: Both lineages use meiosis to reduce homologous sets.
A successful primary spermatocyte lineage produces four spermatids through relatively even divisions.
Oogenesis retains most cytoplasm in one large cell, with polar bodies, and includes characteristic meiotic pauses.
frames.conclusion: Both pathways reduce sets, but their products differ in size, developmental timing and allocation of cytoplasm. An ovulated secondary oocyte typically remains paused in metaphase II.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Sources of variation
frames.scenario: Separate three sources of new combinations: crossing over, independent assortment and random fertilization.
orderedExplanation: Crossing over exchanges corresponding regions between homologous nonsister chromatids.
Independent assortment changes combinations of homologues from different pairs in gametes.
Fertilization combines one gamete from each parent, adding another combination step.
frames.conclusion: These processes reshuffle existing genetic variants at different stages. Mutation is a separate source of new sequence variants and need not occur for every new combination.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Nondisjunction
frames.scenario: In a simple two-division model, homologues of one pair fail to separate in meiosis I. Compare the four gametes with a case in which sister separation fails in one meiosis-II cell.
orderedExplanation: For the meiosis-I error, send both homologues to one first-division product and neither to the other.
After normal meiosis II, obtain two n+1 and two n−1 gametes for that chromosome.
For the stated meiosis-II error, obtain two normal gametes, one n+1 and one n−1.
frames.conclusion: The distribution differs by timing: all four gametes are affected in the simple meiosis-I case, while two remain normal in the specified meiosis-II case.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Twins and early development
frames.scenario: Compare two embryos arising from one fertilized egg that later separates with embryos arising from two separately fertilized eggs.
orderedExplanation: One zygote followed by separation supports a monozygotic origin.
Two oocytes fertilized separately support a dizygotic origin.
Distinguish the origin of genetic similarity from later differences in development, environment and acquired changes.
frames.conclusion: Monozygotic twins arise from one zygote and are usually highly genetically similar. Dizygotic twins arise from separate fertilizations and have a genetic relationship comparable to other full siblings in the stated family model.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

checkpoint.prompt: Does a monozygotic origin guarantee identical traits throughout life?
checkpoint.comparisonGuide: No. Development, environments and later changes can differ despite high genetic similarity.

framing.observableQuestion: How do organisms place meiosis and fertilization in different life cycles?
framing.learningGoal: Compare sexual and asexual strategies and annotate moss, pine and selected animal cycles without merging their distinct stages.
framing.priorKnowledgeSupport: Mitosis preserves the current set number; meiosis reduces it and fertilization restores it. Haploid cells can divide by mitosis. Reproductive success depends on context.

retrieval.prompt: Name the ploidy transitions caused by meiosis and fertilization in a plant cycle.
retrieval.comparisonGuide: Meiosis changes 2n to n; fertilization changes n to 2n. Mitosis preserves the current set number between them.

evidenceSlip.prompt: Compare two reproductive strategies using a specific organism, one mechanism and one environmental tradeoff.

localWalkthrough.status: complete-ordered-narration; illustrations and equivalence review pending

frames.title: Sexual and asexual reproduction
frames.scenario: A fictional plant population can produce runners or seeds after fertilization. Compare inheritance and one ecological tradeoff.
orderedExplanation: Runners develop through mitotic growth from the parent and usually preserve its genotype apart from new changes.
Sexual reproduction combines gametes and can reshuffle parental variants.
Compare speed, resource investment and variation in the stated environment rather than ranking one strategy as universally superior.
frames.conclusion: Asexual propagation can rapidly preserve a successful genotype; sexual reproduction can generate new combinations. Their relative effects depend on conditions, and neither guarantees survival.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Life-cycle transitions
frames.scenario: Trace a moss life cycle from a diploid sporophyte through spores, gametophytes and fertilization. Compare the corresponding ploidy transitions in pine.
orderedExplanation: Meiosis in the diploid sporophyte produces haploid spores.
Spores grow by mitosis into haploid gametophytes, which produce gametes by mitosis.
Fertilization restores diploidy; pine retains these broad transitions with much reduced gametophytes associated with the dominant sporophyte.
frames.conclusion: Meiosis changes 2n to n, fertilization changes n to 2n, and intervening mitosis preserves the current set number. Plant spores and gametes are different stages.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Animal strategies
frames.scenario: Compare a Daphnia model that switches reproductive modes with a jellyfish model containing a polyp stage and a medusa stage. Avoid adding a medusa stage to a sea-anemone cycle.
orderedExplanation: Identify which Daphnia conditions in the supplied model favour asexual or sexual reproduction.
In the jellyfish example, distinguish mitotic asexual production from gamete formation and fertilization.
Treat the sea-anemone example separately because a medusa stage is not part of its life cycle.
frames.conclusion: Different animals can combine reproductive strategies in different sequences. Shared vocabulary does not establish that their complete life cycles are identical.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Evidence and applications
frames.scenario: A fictional nursery compares cloned cuttings with seedlings across a stable treatment and a changing treatment. What would make the comparison informative?
orderedExplanation: Define an outcome such as survival or growth over the same interval.
Replicate groups and control starting size, care and sampling while recording the reproductive origin.
Compare variation and performance separately, then revise a claim that one method must always win.
frames.conclusion: The study can test outcomes under its stated conditions. It cannot establish a universal ranking without evidence across other genotypes and environments.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

checkpoint.prompt: Does a sea-anemone cycle include the jellyfish medusa stage shown in the continuation slide?
checkpoint.comparisonGuide: No. The jellyfish and sea-anemone cycles must remain distinct.

framing.observableQuestion: Why can different genotypes produce the same scored phenotype?
framing.learningGoal: Use genetic notation accurately and distinguish dominance, allele frequency and environmental contributions to traits.
framing.priorKnowledgeSupport: A gene region can have alternative alleles. Diploid individuals carry two copies at a typical autosomal locus. A measured trait depends on a stated expression model.

retrieval.prompt: In complete dominance, which two genotypes can share the dominant phenotype?
retrieval.comparisonGuide: AA and Aa share the scored dominant phenotype while remaining different genotypes.

evidenceSlip.prompt: Correct one claim equating dominant with common, beneficial or environmentally fixed, using the relevant distinction.
criteria: State what evidence would address the other claim.

frames.title: Inheritance language
frames.scenario: In a stated one-locus model, A is completely dominant to a. Translate AA, Aa and aa into genotype and phenotype descriptions.
orderedExplanation: Define the alleles before interpreting the letters.
Identify AA and aa as homozygous and Aa as heterozygous.
Under the stated complete-dominance model, group AA and Aa by the dominant phenotype while retaining distinct genotypes.
frames.conclusion: There are three genotypes but two phenotype categories in this model. The notation does not say which allele is common, beneficial or older.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Trait expression
frames.scenario: A fictional population contains mostly aa individuals even though A is completely dominant. Is the observation contradictory?
orderedExplanation: Use dominance to predict the heterozygote's phenotype.
Use population counts to describe allele or phenotype frequency.
Keep the expression rule separate from the frequency measurement.
frames.conclusion: There is no contradiction. Complete dominance describes expression in a heterozygote; it does not require the dominant allele or phenotype to be common.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Genes and environment
frames.scenario: Two fictional plants share a stated genotype but grow to different heights under different light conditions. Does this disprove inheritance?
orderedExplanation: Identify the shared genotype and the changed environment.
Recognize height as an outcome that can depend on several genes and environmental conditions.
Seek a controlled comparison before attributing the entire difference to light.
frames.conclusion: The observation is compatible with environmental influence on an inherited developmental system. It does not show that genes are irrelevant or that one environmental difference is the only cause.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

checkpoint.prompt: Does a dominant allele have to be the most frequent allele?
checkpoint.comparisonGuide: No. Dominance describes heterozygote expression, not population frequency.

framing.observableQuestion: How can a cross test a model of allele transmission?
framing.learningGoal: Connect segregation with meiosis, define inheritance notation and use offspring observations as probabilistic evidence.
framing.priorKnowledgeSupport: Gametes carry one allele per locus in the model. Phenotype rules must be stated separately from genotype combinations. A small sample need not equal an expected ratio.

retrieval.prompt: What gametes does Aa predict, and with what probabilities under equal transmission?
retrieval.comparisonGuide: A and a, each with probability 1/2 across the stated gamete model.

evidenceSlip.prompt: Use the four-dominant-offspring test-cross case to compare AA and Aa explanations without claiming proof from a small sample.

localWalkthrough.status: complete-ordered-narration; illustrations and equivalence review pending

frames.title: Controlled crosses and evidence
frames.scenario: A fictional true-breeding AA parent is crossed with aa under complete dominance. Predict the first generation, then identify the next cross that tests segregation.
orderedExplanation: Each AA parent gamete carries A and each aa parent gamete carries a.
All first-generation offspring are Aa under this model.
Cross two Aa individuals and compare the next generation with the predicted genotype and phenotype proportions.
frames.conclusion: The first generation is all Aa with the dominant phenotype. Aa × Aa predicts 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa and, under complete dominance, 3 dominant : 1 recessive.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Segregation
frames.scenario: Connect an Aa parent's two allele types with meiosis and its predicted gametes.
orderedExplanation: Place A and a at corresponding loci on homologous chromosomes.
Follow homolog separation during meiosis I and the later separation of sister copies.
Under the stated equal-transmission model, assign probability 1/2 to A and 1/2 to a in a gamete.
frames.conclusion: The two alleles segregate into gametes; a gamete carries one of them at this locus. The 1/2 probabilities are predictions across many gametes, not a guarantee for every small sample.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Inheritance modes and notation
frames.scenario: A supplied model gives heterozygotes a phenotype distinct from both homozygotes. A student applies a 3:1 phenotype ratio to a heterozygote cross. Repair the prediction.
orderedExplanation: Define the three genotype-to-phenotype relationships first.
Construct the heterozygote × heterozygote genotype probabilities: 1/4, 1/2 and 1/4.
Keep the three phenotype categories because the heterozygote does not share either homozygote's phenotype.
frames.conclusion: The phenotype prediction is 1:2:1 in this model. The genotype probabilities do not change merely because the expression relationship differs from complete dominance.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Probability and test crosses
frames.scenario: An individual with a dominant phenotype is crossed with aa. Four observed offspring all have the dominant phenotype. Does this prove that the unknown parent is AA?
orderedExplanation: Compare AA × aa, which predicts all dominant offspring, with Aa × aa, which predicts 1/2 dominant per offspring.
Under independent outcomes, calculate the chance of four dominant offspring from Aa: (1/2)^4 = 1/16.
Use the observation as evidence without treating a possible outcome as impossible.
frames.conclusion: The result is more consistent with AA under the simple alternatives, but it does not prove AA. An Aa parent could produce this small sample with probability 1/16.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

checkpoint.prompt: Do four dominant offspring from a test cross prove the unknown parent is AA?
checkpoint.comparisonGuide: No. An Aa parent can produce that sample with probability 1/16 under the model.

framing.observableQuestion: Which assumptions make a familiar inheritance ratio valid?
framing.learningGoal: Construct mono- and dihybrid crosses, apply probability rules and compare model expectations with supplied samples.
framing.priorKnowledgeSupport: Use the parental genotypes to list the possible gametes, as in the previous lesson. Keep genotype and phenotype separate. Here you will first solve one-locus crosses, then combine independent events, then compare expected and observed results.

retrieval.prompt: For AaBb × AaBb with independent loci, what is P(aaB_)?
retrieval.comparisonGuide: P(aa) × P(B_) = (1/4)(3/4) = 3/16 under the stated model.

evidenceSlip.prompt: Compare one supplied small and large offspring sample with expectations, preserving the denominator and sampling limitation.
criteria: Explain why deviation alone does not prove model failure.

localWalkthrough.status: complete-ordered-narration; illustrations and equivalence review pending

frames.title: Monohybrid crosses
frames.scenario: Solve Aa × Aa under complete dominance, showing genotype and phenotype probabilities separately.
orderedExplanation: List A and a gametes from each parent with probability 1/2.
Combine them to obtain AA, Aa, aA and aa, each with probability 1/4.
Combine Aa and aA as the same heterozygous genotype, then group phenotypes by the stated dominance rule.
frames.conclusion: Genotypes: 1/4 AA, 1/2 Aa, 1/4 aa. Phenotypes: 3/4 dominant and 1/4 recessive.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Probability rules
frames.scenario: For independent loci in AaBb × AaBb with complete dominance, calculate the chance of aaB_ and the chance that exactly one of two independent offspring is aa.
orderedExplanation: Solve the first question one locus at a time. Aa × Aa gives P(aa) = 1/4. Bb × Bb gives P(BB or Bb) = 3/4. B_ means either of these dominant-phenotype genotypes.
The loci are stated to be independent. Multiply the two chances: P(aaB_) = (1/4)(3/4) = 3/16.
For the second question, focus only on the A locus. Each offspring has P(aa) = 1/4 and P(not aa) = 3/4.
List the two orders that meet exactly one: first aa then not aa, or first not aa then aa. Both aa and neither aa do not meet the condition.
The offspring are stated to be independent. Each allowed order has chance (1/4)(3/4) = 3/16.
The two orders cannot occur together. Add their chances: 3/16 + 3/16 = 6/16 = 3/8.
frames.conclusion: The requested probabilities are 3/16 and 3/8. Multiplication uses the stated independence; addition combines non-overlapping alternatives.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Dihybrid crosses
frames.scenario: List gametes from AaBb under independent assortment and predict the phenotype proportions in AaBb × AaBb with complete dominance at both loci.
orderedExplanation: Combine A or a with B or b to obtain AB, Ab, aB and ab, each with probability 1/4.
Combine the two parents' gametes in a 4 × 4 square or multiply single-locus probabilities.
Group the outcomes as A_B_, A_bb, aaB_ and aabb.
frames.conclusion: The predicted phenotype proportions are 9/16, 3/16, 3/16 and 1/16 under the stated assumptions.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Testing a model
frames.scenario: Compare the supplied Aa × Aa genotype counts: small samples 3/5/2 and 1/7/2; large samples 24/51/25 and 28/48/24, ordered AA/Aa/aa.
orderedExplanation: Use 1/4, 1/2 and 1/4 as the model probabilities.
Expected counts are 2.5/5/2.5 for each ten-offspring sample and 25/50/25 for each hundred-offspring sample.
Compare proportions and sample sizes without demanding an exact ratio in each sample.
frames.conclusion: All four samples differ from exact expectations. Such differences alone do not reject the model; interpretation needs sampling variability, replication and checks on the design.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

checkpoint.prompt: Can expected counts of 2.5/5/2.5 occur as literal offspring counts in one ten-offspring family?
checkpoint.comparisonGuide: No. They are model expectations; observed individuals are counted in whole numbers.

framing.observableQuestion: How does the expression model change the phenotype prediction from a cross?

retrieval.prompt: Distinguish incomplete dominance from codominance in the heterozygote.

frames.title: Incomplete dominance
frames.scenario: In a fictional flower model, RR is red, WW is white and RW is pink. Predict RW × RW and explain why the alleles have not permanently blended.
orderedExplanation: List R and W gametes from each parent.
Combine them to obtain 1/4 RR, 1/2 RW and 1/4 WW.
Apply the stated phenotype key to recover red, pink and white offspring categories.
frames.conclusion: The prediction is 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white. Reappearance of both homozygous categories shows that the alleles remain separable rather than being irreversibly blended.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Codominance and multiple alleles
frames.scenario: In the simplified ABO model, cross Iᴬi with Iᴮi. List the possible offspring genotypes and blood-group phenotypes.
orderedExplanation: The first parent supplies Iᴬ or i; the second supplies Iᴮ or i.
Combine to obtain IᴬIᴮ, Iᴬi, Iᴮi and ii, each with probability 1/4.
Apply codominance of Iᴬ and Iᴮ and their dominance over i in this classroom model.
frames.conclusion: The predicted groups are AB, A, B and O, each with probability 1/4. Three allele types exist in the population, while one diploid individual has at most two at this locus.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Sex linkage
frames.scenario: For a stated X-linked recessive model, cross XᴬXᵃ with XᴬY. Calculate the chance of an affected son among all offspring and among sons.
orderedExplanation: List the maternal Xᴬ and Xᵃ gametes and paternal Xᴬ and Y gametes.
The four equally likely outcomes are XᴬXᴬ, XᴬXᵃ, XᴬY and XᵃY in the simplified model.
Count XᵃY once among all four outcomes and once among the two son outcomes.
frames.conclusion: The probability is 1/4 among all offspring and 1/2 conditional on being a son. The denominator changes with the question.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Many genes and environment
frames.scenario: A fictional trait shows a broad continuous distribution rather than two sharply separated categories. What models should be considered before applying a Mendelian ratio?
orderedExplanation: Check whether several loci can contribute to the trait.
Consider environmental variation and measurement effects.
Seek family, genotype or controlled-condition evidence that can distinguish the proposed contributions.
frames.conclusion: A polygenic and environmentally influenced model is plausible, but distribution shape alone does not prove the number of contributing genes.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Comparing model predictions
frames.scenario: A heterozygote cross produces three observed phenotype categories. Compare complete dominance, incomplete dominance and codominance as possible explanations.
orderedExplanation: Ask whether the heterozygote shares a homozygote's phenotype, has an intermediate phenotype or displays both defined products.
Use the observed phenotype definitions to select a model.
Then calculate genotype probabilities and apply that model's phenotype key.
frames.conclusion: The category count alone may suggest that simple complete dominance is inadequate, but the actual phenotype evidence distinguishes incomplete dominance from codominance.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

checkpoint.prompt: Does the same 1:2:1 ratio by itself distinguish incomplete dominance from codominance?
checkpoint.comparisonGuide: No. The nature of the heterozygote phenotype distinguishes the models.

framing.observableQuestion: What can family observations establish, and what must remain conditional?

retrieval.prompt: For an unaffected child of Aa × Aa under a recessive model, what is P(carrier)?

frames.title: Symbols and evidence
frames.scenario: Read a fictional pedigree in which the legend defines filled symbols as a measured phenotype, a horizontal line as a reproductive partnership and a vertical line as descendants. What can be recorded before assigning genotypes?
orderedExplanation: Use the legend to identify relationships and observed phenotype categories.
Assign generation and individual identifiers so evidence can be cited precisely.
Keep unobserved genotypes blank or conditional until an inheritance model supplies constraints.
frames.conclusion: The pedigree records relationships and phenotype observations. Genotypes are inferred under a model and should not be silently treated as directly measured.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Autosomal hypotheses
frames.scenario: Two unaffected fictional parents have an affected child. Under a fully penetrant autosomal recessive model with accurate records, infer the parental and child genotypes.
orderedExplanation: The affected child is aa under the stated model.
Each parent must contribute a.
Because both parents are unaffected in this model, each must also carry A, giving Aa × Aa.
frames.conclusion: The model supports two heterozygous parents and an aa child. It does not establish that every unaffected relative is AA or that this is the only possible real-world explanation.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Sex-linked hypotheses
frames.scenario: A fictional pedigree shows an affected father and an affected son. Does this alone rule out an X-linked recessive explanation?
orderedExplanation: In the stated X-linked model, the father supplies Y to his son rather than the father's X allele.
Check whether the mother could supply the recessive X allele.
Distinguish observed co-occurrence from direct father-to-son transmission of that allele.
frames.conclusion: The pair alone does not rule out X-linked recessive inheritance. An affected son could receive the allele from the mother; more family information is needed.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Risk and information
frames.scenario: An unaffected sibling of an aa child has two Aa parents under a fully penetrant autosomal recessive model. Find the probability that this unaffected sibling is a carrier.
orderedExplanation: Aa × Aa gives AA, Aa, aA and aa with equal probability.
Condition on the sibling being unaffected, removing the aa outcome.
Among the three remaining equally likely outcomes, two are heterozygous.
frames.conclusion: The conditional carrier probability is 2/3. It differs from the unconditioned 1/2 probability of a heterozygote before the phenotype information is used.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

checkpoint.prompt: Does an affected father and son alone prove direct X-linked transmission from father to son?
checkpoint.comparisonGuide: No. In the stated model, the son receives paternal Y and could receive the allele from the mother.

framing.observableQuestion: How much chromosome information can recombinant offspring reveal?
framing.learningGoal: Classify offspring using parental phase, calculate recombination and construct a bounded three-locus map.
framing.priorKnowledgeSupport: Gamete combinations can be parental or recombinant relative to a stated phase. Fractions need all relevant classes and the whole sample. Endpoint observations can miss internal events.

retrieval.prompt: For 80 recombinants among 400 offspring, give the recombinant percentage.
retrieval.comparisonGuide: 80/400 × 100 = 20% recombination; a map-distance estimate requires the stated short-interval assumptions.

evidenceSlip.prompt: Construct the 14/6/20 map, justify the middle locus and state one limit on extending the calculation.
criteria: Place B between A and C.
Mention hidden multiple exchanges or interval assumptions.

frames.title: Linkage and recombination
frames.scenario: A test cross uses an AB/ab heterozygote and an ab/ab partner. Classify AB, ab, Ab and aB gamete-derived offspring types.
orderedExplanation: Read AB and ab as the parental chromosome phase in the heterozygote.
Identify AB and ab as parental combinations.
Identify Ab and aB as recombinant combinations relative to that phase.
frames.conclusion: Parental types are AB and ab; recombinant types are Ab and aB. The same genotype letters written without phase would not supply all this information.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Recombination frequency
frames.scenario: A suitable test cross has 400 offspring: 160 AB, 160 ab, 40 Ab and 40 aB, with parental phase AB/ab. Calculate recombination frequency.
orderedExplanation: Add both recombinant classes: 40 + 40 = 80.
Divide by all offspring: 80/400 = 0.20.
Report 20% recombination and, under the short-interval mapping approximation, about 20 map units.
frames.conclusion: The recombinant fraction is 0.20. Both reciprocal recombinant classes belong in the numerator and every scored offspring belongs in the denominator.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Gene order
frames.scenario: Three loci have supplied short-interval distances A–B = 14, B–C = 6 and A–C = 20 map units. Construct a compatible order.
orderedExplanation: Check that 14 + 6 = 20.
Place B between A and C so the two shorter intervals span the longest interval.
Accept the reversed orientation C—6—B—14—A as the same relative map.
frames.conclusion: A—14—B—6—C is compatible, as is its reverse. The arbitrary left-to-right direction is not a distinct biological result.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Limits of linkage estimates
frames.scenario: Two loci yield about 50% recombinant offspring in a large suitable test cross. Compare two explanations.
orderedExplanation: One possibility is that the loci are on different chromosomes and assort independently.
Another is that they are far apart on the same chromosome, with multiple exchanges obscuring linkage in the two-locus result.
Identify additional linked markers or other evidence that could distinguish the alternatives.
frames.conclusion: The result does not uniquely establish that the loci are on different chromosomes. About 50% is compatible with both explanations in the standard model.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

checkpoint.prompt: Does about 50% recombination prove the loci are on different chromosomes?
checkpoint.comparisonGuide: No. Distant linked loci can also give about 50% in a two-locus comparison.

framing.observableQuestion: How did different observations constrain the DNA model?
framing.learningGoal: Connect historical evidence with DNA's hereditary role and construct complementary antiparallel strands accurately.
framing.priorKnowledgeSupport: An experiment tests a particular claim through comparisons. A nucleotide has sugar, phosphate and base. Sequence order and overall base composition are different information.

retrieval.prompt: Give the aligned complement of 5′-ATGC-3′ with direction labels.
retrieval.comparisonGuide: 3′-TACG-5′ is aligned antiparallel; the same strand written 5′→3′ is 5′-GCAT-3′.

evidenceSlip.prompt: Use one historical experiment or structural observation to state the claim it supports and a claim it did not establish alone.
criteria: Connect it to a specific conclusion.

frames.title: Evidence for hereditary material
frames.scenario: Compare what bacterial transformation, selective enzyme treatment and phage labelling contributed to identifying hereditary material.
orderedExplanation: Transformation showed that material from one bacterial preparation could produce a heritable change in another.
Experiments that selectively disrupted candidate molecules helped test which material was needed for transformation.
Phage labelling distinguished the behaviour of DNA-associated and protein-associated labels during infection.
frames.conclusion: The studies supplied different lines of evidence supporting DNA's hereditary role in the tested systems. One result should not be credited with directly proving every feature of DNA structure or every inheritance mechanism.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Nucleotides and direction
frames.scenario: A diagram shows a phosphate, deoxyribose sugar and nitrogenous base. Identify the nucleotide and explain what 5′ and 3′ labels refer to.
orderedExplanation: Group the three components as one DNA nucleotide.
Locate the sugar's numbered carbon positions used to name the strand ends.
Use those ends to orient the sugar–phosphate backbone rather than assigning direction from the page's left edge alone.
frames.conclusion: A nucleotide contains sugar, phosphate and base. The 5′ and 3′ labels describe chemical orientation, so a sequence must carry direction labels when the diagram's orientation is ambiguous.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Structural evidence
frames.scenario: A double-stranded DNA sample has 30% adenine. Use the stated complementary-pairing model to infer the other base percentages and connect the result to structural evidence.
orderedExplanation: Pair adenine with thymine, giving 30% thymine.
Subtract 60% from the total, leaving 40% for guanine and cytosine together.
Split that remainder equally: 20% each, while recognizing that composition alone does not specify the full three-dimensional structure.
frames.conclusion: T = 30%, G = 20% and C = 20% for this double-stranded sample. Base relationships constrain a model; diffraction evidence and chemical reasoning supplied additional structural constraints.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: The double helix
frames.scenario: Write the strand complementary to 5′-ATGC-3′ first as aligned beneath it, then separately in 5′→3′ notation.
orderedExplanation: Pair A with T and G with C while keeping opposite strand directions.
The aligned complement is 3′-TACG-5′.
Reverse its written order to express that complementary strand from 5′ to 3′: 5′-GCAT-3′.
frames.conclusion: The aligned complement and the reverse-complement notation describe the same strand in different written directions. Both pairing and orientation must be correct.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

checkpoint.prompt: Do equal A and T percentages reveal the exact order of bases?
checkpoint.comparisonGuide: No. Composition constrains totals, while many sequences can share those totals.

framing.observableQuestion: How can both strands be copied when their directions are opposite?
framing.learningGoal: Trace semiconservative copying, enzyme roles and leading/lagging synthesis, then compare density-model predictions.
framing.priorKnowledgeSupport: DNA strands are complementary and antiparallel. New strands grow from a suitable end. Strand age, chemical direction and fork movement need separate labels.

retrieval.prompt: Which direction does new DNA grow on both leading and lagging products?
retrieval.comparisonGuide: Both grow 5′→3′; the lagging product forms fragments relative to fork movement.

evidenceSlip.prompt: Use a fork diagram or density model to explain a replication prediction and a condition needed to interpret it.
criteria: State direction, round or model assumptions.

frames.title: Semiconservative replication
frames.scenario: Begin with one DNA duplex whose two strands are labelled old. Follow two rounds of semiconservative replication using new unlabelled nucleotides.
orderedExplanation: After the first round, form two duplexes, each with one old strand and one new strand.
Separate each duplex's strands for the second round and use each as a template.
Count four duplexes: two retain one original old strand, while two contain only strands made after the start.
frames.conclusion: After two rounds, two of four duplexes contain an original old strand. No duplex retains both original strands paired together in this model.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Enzymes and direction
frames.scenario: A template is oriented 3′→5′ along the direction a polymerase is reading. State the direction of new DNA synthesis and the role of a primer.
orderedExplanation: Use complementary pairing to choose the next base.
Add nucleotides to the available 3′ end of the growing new strand.
Recognize that DNA polymerase extends a suitable primer rather than starting a new strand without that initial end.
frames.conclusion: The new strand grows 5′→3′ while the template is read 3′→5′. Primers provide a starting end for extension in the replication model.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Leading and lagging synthesis
frames.scenario: At a fork moving right, the upper template runs 3′→5′ from left to right and the lower template runs 5′→3′. Identify the continuous new-strand direction and the fragment direction.
orderedExplanation: On the upper template, new DNA can grow 5′→3′ toward the moving fork.
On the lower template, each new fragment still grows 5′→3′ but away from the fork over the locally exposed region.
Repeated initiation allows fragments to be produced as more template is exposed.
frames.conclusion: The upper-template product is leading in this defined fork view; the lower-template product is lagging. Both products use 5′→3′ synthesis, with different arrangements relative to fork movement.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Replication evidence
frames.scenario: In a simplified density-labelling experiment, DNA begins heavy and is then copied in light medium. Compare semiconservative predictions after one and two rounds.
orderedExplanation: After one round, predict duplexes with one heavy original strand and one light new strand, producing an intermediate-density class.
After two rounds, predict half intermediate and half light duplexes.
Compare this sequence with alternative models rather than treating one intermediate result as the entire test.
frames.conclusion: The two-round pattern supports the semiconservative model under the experiment's conditions. The first round alone does not distinguish every possible alternative.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

checkpoint.prompt: Does semiconservative replication make each new strand half old and half new?
checkpoint.comparisonGuide: No. After one round, each daughter duplex pairs a pre-existing strand with a new strand.

framing.observableQuestion: Which strand is read, and why does direction change the answer?
framing.learningGoal: Identify a gene's template, transcribe an oriented sequence and distinguish RNA processing from changes to DNA.
framing.priorKnowledgeSupport: Complementary pairing links two strands with opposite directions. The coding strand matches RNA base order except T/U. A short supplied region need not be a complete gene.

retrieval.prompt: Transcribe template 3′-TAC CTT-5′ with RNA direction labels.
retrieval.comparisonGuide: 5′-AUG GAA-3′.

evidenceSlip.prompt: Correct a strand-orientation or processing claim by showing the relevant sequence and explaining the error.
criteria: Use correct direction and RNA bases.
Distinguish transcription/processing from translation or DNA removal.

frames.title: Selecting a template
frames.scenario: A gene's coding strand is 5′-ATG GAA TTT TAA-3′. Identify the aligned template and the corresponding RNA sequence in the stated orientation.
orderedExplanation: Pair an antiparallel template: 3′-TAC CTT AAA ATT-5′.
Read that template 3′→5′.
Build RNA 5′→3′ using complementary bases, with U in place of T.
frames.conclusion: The RNA is 5′-AUG GAA UUU UAA-3′. It matches the coding strand's base order except for U replacing T.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Making RNA
frames.scenario: Transcribe the template 3′-TAC CTT AAA ATT-5′ into RNA and state the base-pairing choices.
orderedExplanation: Read the template in its given 3′→5′ direction.
Pair T with A, A with U, C with G and G with C in RNA.
Write the resulting strand 5′→3′ and retain the complete sequence.
frames.conclusion: The transcript is 5′-AUG GAA UUU UAA-3′. Transcription creates RNA; the amino-acid sequence is a separate later interpretation.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Processing and expression
frames.scenario: A simplified eukaryotic precursor RNA contains exon 1, intron 1 and exon 2. Describe the processed RNA without claiming that every exon base must encode an amino acid.
orderedExplanation: Identify the intron region marked for removal in the stated model.
Join the retained exon regions through splicing.
Keep untranslated regions and other processing features conceptually distinct from the protein-coding portion.
frames.conclusion: The processed transcript retains the joined exon sequence, while the intron is removed in this example. Exons can include untranslated regions, so exon and protein-coding sequence are not identical terms.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Checking a sequence claim
frames.scenario: A student transcribes 3′-TAC CTT-5′ as 5′-UAC CUU-3′. Locate the error and repair the sequence.
orderedExplanation: Notice that the student replaced T with U while copying the template directly.
Apply complementary pairing to the template instead.
Read its stated 3′→5′ direction to obtain the new RNA 5′→3′.
frames.conclusion: The correct RNA is 5′-AUG GAA-3′. Direct T-to-U substitution applies to a matching coding-strand sequence, not to this template.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

checkpoint.prompt: Can you copy a template strand unchanged and merely replace T with U?
checkpoint.comparisonGuide: No. RNA must be complementary to the template in the correct direction.

framing.observableQuestion: What does a codon table predict, and what does it leave unknown?
framing.learningGoal: Translate a supplied RNA frame, explain tRNA/ribosome roles and distinguish peptide sequence from functional evidence.
framing.priorKnowledgeSupport: mRNA is read in a defined 5′→3′ frame. Codons are RNA triplets. Complementary anticodons are antiparallel, and a stop signal is not an amino acid.

retrieval.prompt: Translate AUG GAA UUU UAA in the stated frame.
retrieval.comparisonGuide: Met–Glu–Phe, followed by termination at UAA.

evidenceSlip.prompt: Use a short sequence to support a peptide prediction, then state what further evidence a protein-function claim needs.
criteria: Show the correct frame and peptide.
Handle stop or trailing bases correctly.
