frames.title: Reading the genetic code
frames.scenario: Translate the supplied complete coding-region model RNA 5′-AUG GAA UUU UAA-3′ from its stated start codon.
orderedExplanation: Read mRNA codons in the 5′→3′ direction using the RNA codon table.
Map AUG to methionine, GAA to glutamate and UUU to phenylalanine.
Treat UAA as a termination signal rather than an amino acid.
frames.conclusion: The peptide sequence is Met–Glu–Phe, followed by termination at UAA in this model.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Adaptors and peptide bonds
frames.scenario: For mRNA codon 5′-GAA-3′, write an aligned anticodon and identify the role of the charged tRNA.
orderedExplanation: Pair the anticodon antiparallel to the codon: 3′-CUU-5′.
Recognize that a correctly charged tRNA carries the corresponding amino acid, glutamate in the standard code.
Connect codon recognition with peptide-bond formation at the ribosome.
frames.conclusion: The aligned anticodon is 3′-CUU-5′, or 5′-UUC-3′ when written in its own 5′→3′ direction. The adaptor links RNA recognition with delivery of an amino acid.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Initiation to termination
frames.scenario: Sequence initiation, elongation and termination for a model transcript with an AUG start and a later UGA in the same reading frame.
orderedExplanation: Establish the translation machinery and reading frame at the supplied start region.
Add amino acids as successive codons are read during elongation.
Use the in-frame stop codon to recruit termination machinery and release the peptide.
frames.conclusion: Translation proceeds through a defined frame until a stop signal is reached. UGA does not require a normal tRNA carrying a “stop amino acid.”
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: From sequence to function
frames.scenario: Translate 5′-AUG GAA UUU UAA-3′, then evaluate the claim that the sequence alone proves a functional enzyme.
orderedExplanation: Use the standard code to obtain Met–Glu–Phe followed by stop.
Distinguish this short classroom peptide model from a complete functional protein.
Identify additional evidence about folding, processing, localization and activity that would address function.
frames.conclusion: The sequence supports the stated translation result. It does not establish enzyme activity or the complete behaviour of a protein in a cell.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

checkpoint.prompt: Does an out-of-frame UGA necessarily stop the current translation?
checkpoint.comparisonGuide: No. Only codons in the established reading frame are read as that sequence progresses.

framing.observableQuestion: Why can different sequence changes have very different consequences?
framing.learningGoal: Trace substitution and insertion examples through expression while separating origin, transmission and selection.
framing.priorKnowledgeSupport: DNA sequence, RNA sequence and peptide sequence are linked but distinct. Coding context and frame determine triplet interpretation. Somatic and germline lineages have different inheritance routes.

retrieval.prompt: Why do GAA and GAG yield the same amino acid in the supplied standard-code model?
retrieval.comparisonGuide: Both codons specify glutamate, so that substitution is synonymous for the peptide sequence.

evidenceSlip.prompt: Compare one reference and variant sequence, show its defined consequence and keep one untested effect or downstream region unknown.
criteria: Do not invent a stop, full protein or universal harmful effect.

frames.title: Types of sequence change
frames.scenario: Compare coding DNA reference ATGGAATTTTAA with substitution ATGGAGTTTTAA and insertion ATGAGAATTTTAA in the stated frame beginning at the first base.
orderedExplanation: The substitution changes one base without changing the total length.
The insertion adds one base after ATG, changing later triplet grouping.
Separate the type of sequence change from its effect on the translated product.
frames.conclusion: The substitution preserves the reading frame; the one-base insertion shifts downstream grouping in this coding-region model. Neither label alone determines every functional effect.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Effects on gene products
frames.scenario: Compare translation of the reference coding DNA ATGGAATTTTAA and the substitution ATGGAGTTTTAA in the supplied standard-code model.
orderedExplanation: Convert coding DNA to matching RNA with T replaced by U.
Read reference AUG GAA UUU UAA and variant AUG GAG UUU UAA in the same frame.
Use the code table to note that GAA and GAG both specify glutamate.
frames.conclusion: Both produce Met–Glu–Phe followed by stop in this model. The substitution is synonymous for this peptide sequence, which does not prove that every possible regulatory or expression effect is absent.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Inheritance and variation
frames.scenario: A fictional sequence change occurs in one skin-cell lineage, while a separate change occurs in a cell lineage contributing to gametes. Compare their potential inheritance.
orderedExplanation: Track the skin-cell change through its descendant somatic cells.
Track the gamete-lineage change into possible reproductive cells.
Distinguish the origin of a variant from later selection on carriers and from whether a particular gamete participates in fertilization.
frames.conclusion: A somatic change is generally confined to that lineage and is not normally inherited through gametes. A germline change can be transmitted if it enters a gamete that contributes to offspring.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Evaluating mutation evidence
frames.scenario: Translate the insertion sequence's coding-region excerpt ATGAGAATTTTAA in the stated frame and compare it with the reference ATGGAATTTTAA.
orderedExplanation: The insertion RNA is AUGAGAAUUUUAA.
Group complete codons from the first base: AUG AGA AUU UUA, with one trailing A.
Translate Met–Arg–Ile–Leu and report that no stop codon is supplied in this short shifted frame.
frames.conclusion: The insertion changes the peptide segment and leaves an incomplete trailing codon. Do not invent a downstream stop or claim this excerpt defines the full variant protein.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

checkpoint.prompt: Does a one-base insertion excerpt without an in-frame stop let us invent the final full peptide length?
checkpoint.comparisonGuide: No. Unprovided downstream sequence remains unknown.

frames.title: Cutting and joining DNA
frames.scenario: A fictional linear 1000-base DNA fragment has one defined cut producing 400- and 600-base products. Predict the count and total length, then contrast a one-cut circular molecule.
orderedExplanation: For the linear molecule, one internal cut creates two pieces.
Check conservation: 400 + 600 = 1000 bases.
For a circular molecule, one cut opens the circle into one linear piece rather than creating two separate pieces.
frames.conclusion: The linear case gives two fragments totalling 1000 bases. The one-cut circular case gives one linear molecule of the original total length.

frames.title: Transforming cells
frames.scenario: A fictional recombinant-DNA workflow joins an insert to a vector, introduces the material into cells and selects surviving colonies. Does survival alone prove the intended insert is correct and expressed?
orderedExplanation: Separate joining, cellular uptake and selection as different steps.
Identify exactly what the selection marker tests in the supplied model.
Use additional checks for insert presence, orientation, sequence and expression as needed for the claim.
frames.conclusion: Selection can identify cells with a relevant marker, but it does not by itself prove a correct functional insert. Appropriate positive, negative and identity checks remain necessary.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Amplifying and separating
frames.scenario: A fictional PCR lane shows no target band. Compare “the target is absent” with “the assay failed,” then identify needed controls.
orderedExplanation: Recognize that no visible band can result from either missing target or failure of amplification/detection.
Check a positive control for assay function and a negative control for contamination.
Consider sample-specific quality or an appropriate internal control before concluding absence.
frames.conclusion: The negative lane is consistent with absence or assay failure until controls narrow the alternatives. In a gel, interpret migration against the stated size standard and method resolution.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Genetic evidence and relatedness
frames.scenario: Three fictional sequences of the same region differ from a reference at one, three and six aligned positions. What relationship claim can this comparison support?
orderedExplanation: Confirm that the same homologous region and alignment are being compared.
Count differences using one stated rule and equal sequence coverage.
Treat fewer differences as evidence of closer similarity for this region, while retaining sampling and evolutionary-model limits.
frames.conclusion: The one-difference sequence is most similar to the reference in the compared region. This alone does not establish a complete family relationship or the history of the whole genome.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Applications and uncertainty
frames.scenario: A fictional report claims that a matching DNA pattern proves identity and guilt and that a crop technology is automatically sustainable. Identify the evidence missing from both claims.
orderedExplanation: For the DNA claim, examine sample provenance, contamination, match interpretation and the distinction between biological association and conduct.
For the crop claim, define outcomes such as yield, resource use and ecological effects over a stated interval.
Compare alternatives and ethical, cultural, social and economic perspectives rather than treating a mechanism as a complete verdict.
frames.conclusion: A DNA match is evidence requiring context; it is not itself proof of guilt. Sustainability is a multi-outcome claim requiring measured comparisons and stated values, not a property established by a technology label alone.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

checkpoint.prompt: Does colony survival after selection alone prove a correct expressed insert?
checkpoint.comparisonGuide: No. The marker may not establish insert sequence, orientation or expression.

framing.observableQuestion: When can allele frequencies be counted directly, and when are they inferred through a model?
framing.learningGoal: Calculate allele and genotype frequencies with correct denominators and distinguish observations from equilibrium expectations.
framing.priorKnowledgeSupport: A diploid individual has two allele copies at an autosomal locus. For a frequency, divide the part by the matching whole. Start by counting copies directly. Then use the model to connect allele frequencies with expected genotypes. The worked example shows each square-root step.

retrieval.prompt: From 36 AA, 48 Aa and 16 aa, calculate p.
retrieval.comparisonGuide: A copies = 2(36) + 48 = 120; all copies = 200, so p = 0.60.

evidenceSlip.prompt: Solve one supplied population case and state whether its allele frequency was counted or inferred, including a relevant assumption.
criteria: Show the denominator or q² step.
Label observed versus expected and state a model limit.

localWalkthrough.status: complete-ordered-narration; illustrations and equivalence review pending

frames.title: Populations and allele counts
frames.scenario: A diploid population sample contains 36 AA, 48 Aa and 16 aa individuals. Calculate A and a allele counts and frequencies directly from the observations.
orderedExplanation: Count 100 individuals and therefore 200 allele copies at this autosomal locus.
Count A copies: 2(36) + 48 = 120; count a copies: 2(16) + 48 = 80.
Divide each count by 200 to obtain p = 0.60 and q = 0.40.
frames.conclusion: The observed allele frequencies are 0.60 and 0.40. Direct counting does not require assuming Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Allele and genotype frequencies
frames.scenario: Using p = 0.60 and q = 0.40, calculate Hardy–Weinberg expected genotype frequencies and compare them with the observed 36/48/16 sample.
orderedExplanation: Calculate p² = 0.36, 2pq = 0.48 and q² = 0.16.
Check that the three expected frequencies sum to 1.
Compare with observed genotype frequencies 36/100, 48/100 and 16/100 while keeping observed and expected labels separate.
frames.conclusion: The observed frequencies match these expectations in this sample. That numerical match alone does not prove that every equilibrium condition holds or that the frequencies will remain constant across generations.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Equilibrium assumptions
frames.scenario: A large population mates randomly at one locus but receives immigrants carrying a different allele frequency. Which part of the Hardy–Weinberg model is challenged?
orderedExplanation: Identify gene flow as movement of alleles into the population.
Recognize that random mating does not cancel a change in allele frequencies caused by immigration.
Separate conditions affecting genotype arrangement from conditions maintaining allele frequencies across generations.
frames.conclusion: The no-migration condition is violated. The population could form genotype proportions near p²:2pq:q² after random mating while its p and q have changed through gene flow.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Solving and checking
frames.scenario: In a fictional fully penetrant recessive-trait model, 9% of a population shows the recessive phenotype. Assuming Hardy–Weinberg conditions, estimate q, p and the carrier frequency.
orderedExplanation: Identify the observed group: 9% show the recessive phenotype. Under the stated assumptions, that group is aa and its fraction is q².
Convert percent to a fraction: 9/100 = 0.09, so q² = 0.09.
Find the number whose square is 0.09. Since 0.30 × 0.30 = 0.09, q = 0.30.
Use p + q = 1. Subtract 0.30 from one to get p = 0.70.
Carriers are heterozygotes. Their expected fraction is 2pq = 2(0.70)(0.30) = 0.42, or 42%.
Check the whole: p² + 2pq + q² = 0.49 + 0.42 + 0.09 = 1. The genotype fractions account for the complete population.
frames.conclusion: The estimated allele frequencies are q = 0.30 and p = 0.70; the expected carrier frequency is 0.42. These are model-based estimates, not directly counted genotypes.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: A model and its limits
frames.scenario: A sample contains 45 AA, 45 Aa and 10 aa individuals. Calculate p directly and compare the observed genotype frequencies with Hardy–Weinberg expectations.
orderedExplanation: Count A copies: 90 + 45 = 135 out of 200, so p = 0.675 and q = 0.325.
Calculate expectations p² = 0.455625, 2pq = 0.43875 and q² = 0.105625.
Compare with observed frequencies 0.45, 0.45 and 0.10 without demanding exact equality in a finite sample.
frames.conclusion: The direct allele count gives p = 0.675. The small observed–expected differences require an appropriate sampling and model assessment before supporting a claim of a particular evolutionary cause.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

checkpoint.prompt: Does direct allele counting from observed diploid genotypes require equilibrium?
checkpoint.comparisonGuide: No. It uses the observed copies; equilibrium is needed for particular predictions or inference shortcuts.

framing.observableQuestion: How can the same frequency change arise through different mechanisms?
framing.learningGoal: Separate mutation, selection, drift, movement and mating effects, using supplied population data to compare explanations.
framing.priorKnowledgeSupport: Allele frequencies track copies across a defined population. Genotype proportions can change without changing allele totals. A trend alone does not establish its cause.

retrieval.prompt: Do the sampled p values 0.60, 0.675 and 0.65 show a steady rise?
retrieval.comparisonGuide: No. They rise and then decline; the mechanism also remains unresolved from those counts alone.

evidenceSlip.prompt: Revise a selection or resistance claim with a measured frequency change, a mechanism and one alternative needing evidence.

frames.title: Mutation and selection
frames.scenario: A fictional bacterial population contains a rare resistance variant before an antibiotic exposure. Its frequency later rises. Separate variant origin from the change in representation.
orderedExplanation: Identify mutation or prior inheritance as the source of the existing variant.
During exposure, compare survival and reproduction of carriers and non-carriers.
Explain the later frequency change through differential contribution to descendants rather than need-directed mutation.
frames.conclusion: Selection can increase a pre-existing resistance variant's representation. The exposure does not show that bacteria intentionally produced the exact mutation they needed.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Chance and population size
frames.scenario: Two simulated populations begin with p = 0.50. One samples ten reproductive contributors and the other samples one thousand. Predict which is more likely to show large random frequency swings and distinguish founder and bottleneck cases.
orderedExplanation: Recognize random sampling as the mechanism in both simulations.
A smaller sample generally shows larger proportional fluctuations.
A founder event samples colonists from a source; a bottleneck sharply reduces an existing population before later recovery.
frames.conclusion: The smaller population is more prone to large random swings in this model. Founder and bottleneck effects are different histories that can both intensify drift.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Movement and mating
frames.scenario: A receiving population has 100 diploid individuals with p = 0.60. Ten immigrants each carry AA. Calculate the new allele frequency before reproduction, then contrast a change in mating pattern alone.
orderedExplanation: The original population has 120 A copies among 200 total copies.
Add 20 A copies from ten AA immigrants, giving 140/220.
Calculate p ≈ 0.6364; a mating-pattern change without differential reproduction or other forces can instead alter genotype proportions while leaving allele counts unchanged.
frames.conclusion: Immigration changes p to about 0.6364 in this model. Non-random mating alone need not change p and q, even when it changes heterozygote frequency.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Resistance and evidence
frames.scenario: An antibiotic-exposed sample becomes enriched for a resistance allele. A comparison sample also changes, but it passed through a severe random bottleneck. What evidence could separate selection from drift?
orderedExplanation: Compare replicated exposed and unexposed groups under similar sampling conditions.
Measure whether the allele is associated with differential survival or reproduction during exposure.
Track bottlenecks and starting frequencies so random sampling remains an explicit alternative.
frames.conclusion: A repeated exposure-linked advantage would support selection more directly than a frequency change alone. A bottleneck can change frequencies by chance and must be considered.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Testing explanations
frames.scenario: The supplied population samples are 36/48/16, 45/45/10 and 42/46/12 for AA/Aa/aa. Calculate p for each and evaluate “the allele rose steadily because of selection.”
orderedExplanation: Use the two-copy denominator in each 100-individual sample.
Calculate p values 0.60, 0.675 and 0.65.
Notice the rise followed by a decline, then ask what evidence distinguishes selection from drift, migration and sampling.
frames.conclusion: The allele did not rise steadily. The observations show a changing sampled frequency, while the cause remains unresolved without further evidence.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

checkpoint.prompt: Can non-random mating alone alter genotype proportions without changing p and q?
checkpoint.comparisonGuide: Yes, under the stated model without other forces or differential reproductive contribution.

framing.observableQuestion: How do boundaries, units and time affect a population-growth answer?
framing.learningGoal: Estimate abundance and density, calculate demographic change and rates, and compare bounded growth models.
framing.priorKnowledgeSupport: Counts, area and elapsed time have different units. Population gains and losses must use one boundary and interval. A model equation expresses specified assumptions, not every cause.

retrieval.prompt: From N₀ = 1000, B = 120, I = 30, D = 70 and E = 20 over ten days, give final N and absolute daily change.
retrieval.comparisonGuide: Final N = 1060; absolute change rate = 60/10 = 6 individuals/day.

evidenceSlip.prompt: Use a sampling or growth calculation to support a prediction, including units and one design/model limit.

localWalkthrough.status: complete-ordered-narration; illustrations and equivalence review pending

frames.title: Size and density
frames.scenario: A fictional area contains 240 individuals in 12 hectares. Calculate density and explain why the same density could occur in a population of a different total size.
orderedExplanation: Divide the count by area: 240/12 = 20.
Attach units: 20 individuals per hectare.
Construct a comparison such as 100 individuals in 5 hectares, also 20 per hectare, while retaining different population totals.
frames.conclusion: Density is 20 individuals/ha. Equal density does not imply equal total population size or identical spatial arrangement.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Sampling populations
frames.scenario: Five one-square-metre quadrats contain 2, 8, 4, 10 and 6 individuals. Estimate abundance in a comparable 200 m² habitat.
orderedExplanation: Add the counts: 30 individuals across 5 m².
Calculate mean density: 30/5 = 6 individuals/m².
Multiply by 200 m² to estimate 1200 individuals, assuming the sample represents the habitat.
frames.conclusion: The estimate is 1200 individuals. It is not a complete census; patchiness, sampling placement and detection can affect its reliability.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Four demographic processes
frames.scenario: A population starts at 1000. Over ten days it records 120 births, 30 immigrants, 70 deaths and 20 emigrants. Calculate net change and final size.
orderedExplanation: Add gains: 120 + 30 = 150.
Add losses: 70 + 20 = 90.
Subtract to obtain ΔN = 60, then add to the starting size: 1060.
frames.conclusion: The net change is +60 individuals and the final population size is 1060 under this complete-count model.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Rates and denominators
frames.scenario: Use ΔN = 60, initial N = 1000 and Δt = 10 days to calculate absolute daily change, interval per-initial-individual change and its daily average.
orderedExplanation: Calculate ΔN/Δt = 60/10 = 6 individuals/day.
Calculate ΔN/Ninitial = 60/1000 = 0.06 over the interval.
Divide the interval value by ten to obtain an average 0.006 per day per initial individual.
frames.conclusion: The three summaries are 6 individuals/day, 0.06 per initial individual over ten days, and 0.006 per day per initial individual. The last is an average based on the initial denominator, not a directly fitted continuous intrinsic rate.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Exponential and logistic models
frames.scenario: Compare two discrete models starting at N = 100 with r = 0.2 per step: exponential Nnext = N + rN and logistic Nnext = N + rN(1 − N/K), with K = 500.
orderedExplanation: Exponential next size is 100 + 0.2(100) = 120.
Compare the density-dependent factor while retaining the same initial size, step and r.
frames.conclusion: The first step gives 120 versus 116. In the logistic model, the additional factor reduces growth as N approaches the stated K.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Feedback and changing limits
frames.scenario: A fictional population initially stabilizes near 500, but a drought reduces available habitat and resources. Evaluate the claim that its carrying capacity must remain 500 forever.
orderedExplanation: Identify K as a model summary of support under particular conditions.
Link the environmental change to altered resource availability and possibly a different effective K.
Consider delayed population responses and other losses rather than forcing the old curve onto the new conditions.
frames.conclusion: The earlier value need not remain valid. A changing environment can alter the support conditions, and the population may respond with delays or fluctuations.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

checkpoint.prompt: Are 6 individuals/day and 0.006 per day per initial individual the same numerical quantity?
checkpoint.comparisonGuide: No. They summarize the same change with different denominators and units.

framing.observableQuestion: How do interactions and history shape a community's possible future?
framing.learningGoal: Compare life histories, interaction mechanisms, cycles and succession, then make a qualified ecological recommendation.
framing.priorKnowledgeSupport: An interaction's effect must be measured for each partner. Correlation differs from a causal mechanism. Communities carry biological and environmental legacies after disturbance.

retrieval.prompt: Why does soil remaining after disturbance matter when distinguishing primary and secondary succession?
retrieval.comparisonGuide: Retained soil and biological legacies change starting conditions and can support recovery pathways unlike development on bare rock.

criteria: Connect it to a plausible mechanism or action.

frames.title: Life-history strategies
frames.scenario: Compare a fictional species producing many small offspring with little parental care and another producing fewer offspring with greater investment. Use r/K language cautiously.
orderedExplanation: Describe the measured traits rather than beginning with a fixed label.
Relate offspring number, size, timing and survival under the stated conditions.
Use r- and K-associated tendencies as an idealized comparison while allowing mixed traits and environmental context.
frames.conclusion: The species show contrasting investment patterns, but real life histories occupy continua. A few traits do not place every organism into two rigid universal boxes.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Interactions and their effects
frames.scenario: Classify three fictional interactions: both partners show improved reproductive output; one benefits while the other's measured outcome is unchanged; one benefits while the other is harmed.
orderedExplanation: Use the defined measured effect for each partner.
Assign +/+ to mutualism, +/0 to commensalism and +/− to an antagonistic interaction such as parasitism or predation depending on mechanism.
Avoid choosing a precise mechanism solely from the signs.
frames.conclusion: The effect pattern helps classify the relationship, while the biological mechanism distinguishes interactions sharing the same sign pattern.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Competition and defence
frames.scenario: The supplied plant comparison gives mean A mass 4.0 in five-A pots, 3.0 in ten-A pots and 2.4 in mixed five-A/five-B pots. What comparisons address density and neighbour identity?
orderedExplanation: Compare five-A with ten-A pots for an intraspecific density contrast.
Compare ten-A with mixed pots at ten total plants to hold total density constant while changing neighbour composition.
Retain replication and resource measurements as limits on a specific causal claim.
frames.conclusion: The mixed pots have lower mean A mass than the same-total-density A-only pots. This supports a neighbour-composition effect in the dataset, while the exact resource mechanism requires more evidence.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Population cycles
frames.scenario: A fictional prey curve peaks before a predator curve. Explain a plausible interaction and an alternative cause that the graph alone cannot exclude.
orderedExplanation: Read the time axis and identify the lag between sampled peaks.
Propose that increased prey availability supports later predator reproduction or survival.
Consider shared environmental drivers, other prey and sampling effects before claiming a unique cause.
frames.conclusion: The lag is consistent with a predator–prey interaction, but correlation and timing alone do not prove that this mechanism fully explains the cycle.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Succession and disturbance
frames.scenario: Compare community development on newly exposed rock with recovery after a fire that leaves soil and some surviving organisms. Avoid predicting one inevitable final community.
orderedExplanation: Use the absence of developed soil as a key feature of the primary-succession example.
Use retained soil and biological legacies in the secondary-succession example.
Compare colonization, dispersal, conditions and later disturbance as influences on the pathways.
frames.conclusion: The two starting conditions support different recovery processes and timescales. Neither case guarantees a universal fixed climax community.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Ecological decisions and communication
frames.scenario: A fictional Canadian wetland project proposes restoration based on one season of higher plant abundance. What evidence would strengthen a recommendation?
orderedExplanation: Define the intended outcomes, including biodiversity, water conditions and relevant community priorities.
Compare with suitable reference or untreated sites across enough time to address seasonal variation.
Record sampling methods, possible tradeoffs and Indigenous and local perspectives through appropriate respectful engagement rather than inventing agreement.
frames.conclusion: One season's abundance result supports a limited observation, not complete restoration success. A recommendation should connect measured outcomes with uncertainties, alternatives and the perspectives needed for the decision.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

checkpoint.prompt: Does higher abundance of one plant automatically show greater biodiversity?
checkpoint.comparisonGuide: No. Abundance of one species and diversity are different outcomes that need separate measurements.

seminar.title: Review Seminar: connect the evidence
introduction: Reproduction links cell processes, organs, signals and developmental events. A system diagram should show what each arrow means: movement through a duct, a hormone reaching a target, or feedback changing a signal. Evidence at one step does not establish every later step. Sort the observation by place, scale and timing before selecting a mechanism.

An evidence ledger keeps the observation, source, units or categories, timing and uncertainty visible. Put inferred events in a separate column. A later outcome cannot by itself prove an earlier cause. Compare more than one explanation and identify an observation that would distinguish them.

A classroom recommendation should identify what to measure, compare or verify next. Consider access, consent, privacy and other affected perspectives when evaluating how evidence might be used. It should not prescribe treatment or decide anyone’s reproductive choices. A strong conclusion can remain provisional if it explains what new result would change it.

activities.prompt: Connect one mechanism from each model in three short cause-and-effect statements. Label movement, hormonal influence or development; keep the three model sources separate.
activities.modelResponse: Transport: blockage reduces downstream passage despite upstream cells. Cycle: lower progesterone support can lead to endometrial shedding. Development: a blastocyst can attach only under suitable uterine conditions. Separate models.

activities.prompt: Evaluate the claim that these observations prove a single cause of failed implantation. Distinguish direct observations from inferences and name one useful additional measurement.
activities.modelResponse: No implantation failure was recorded, and the observations come from separate models. A blocked duct explains its own transport result, not every later outcome. Observe attachment in the developmental model under defined conditions.
criteria: No invented outcome or joined dataset

activities.prompt: Revise the claim after a peer points out the different sources. State the next evidence step and one consideration for responsible use of reproductive information.
activities.modelResponse: Each model supports a limited mechanism; together they do not diagnose a person. Keep sources separate and test attachment with a suitable comparison. Any use of personal reproductive information requires informed consent and privacy.
criteria: Consent, privacy or another justified perspective

options.2: The prompt supplies only four offspring, so the unequal classes have no useful interpretation.
options.3: Linked alleles can never be separated by recombination.

otherActivityRecords.title: Why is father-to-son transmission incompatible with a simple X-linked locus?

options.0: A father contributes a Y rather than an X chromosome to a son in the simplified model
options.1: Fathers never contribute chromosomes
options.2: Sons inherit both X chromosomes from the father
options.3: X-linked alleles disappear in sperm

otherActivityRecords.title: A fictional pedigree shows an affected father and an affected son. The mother’s genotype is unknown. Does this pair alone rule out an X-linked recessive model?

options.0: No; the son could have inherited the relevant X allele from his mother.
options.1: Yes; an affected father and son prove direct transfer of the paternal X.
options.2: The pair alone proves mitochondrial inheritance.
options.3: The pair proves the mother cannot carry the relevant X allele.

otherActivityRecords.title: Under a fully penetrant X-linked recessive model, a carrier mother XᴿXʳ and an unaffected father XᴿY have a child. Assume equal probabilities of an X- or Y-bearing sperm. What is the probability of an affected son among all offspring?
In the lesson’s simplified XY model, molecular evidence establishes direct father-to-son inheritance of the same allele. Why does this conflict with the proposed X-linked route?

options.0: The father passes Y rather than his X to a son in this model.
options.1: The father passes his X to every son.
options.2: A father cannot pass any autosomal allele to a son.
options.3: All paternal alleles must be located on the Y chromosome.

otherActivityRecords.title: How is recombination frequency calculated in a test cross?

options.0: Total recombinant offspring divided by total offspring, multiplied by 100 percent
options.1: Parental offspring divided only by recombinants
options.2: Map units divided by chromosome number
options.3: Dominant phenotypes divided by recessive phenotypes

otherActivityRecords.title: A test cross has 92 recombinant offspring among 1,000 total. Which explanation best connects this evidence to the lesson mechanism?

options.0: The estimated distance is 9.2 map units, assuming the recombinant classes are correctly identified and similarly viable.
options.1: The loci behave as effectively unlinked in this dataset; they may be on different chromosomes or far apart on one chromosome.
options.2: The pattern supports M as the middle locus, with adjacent interval calculations needed for the map.
options.3: The genes are exactly 9.2 DNA bases apart.

otherActivityRecords.title: Two loci show 49% recombination in a large two-point cross. Which additional evidence would distinguish different chromosomes from widely separated loci on one chromosome?

options.0: Physical chromosome locations or linkage to intervening markers
options.1: The same two-point percentage rounded to 50%
options.2: A total count of offspring without marker genotypes
options.3: A statement that 1% recombination always equals one DNA base

otherActivityRecords.title: A two-point cross has 486 recombinants among 1,000 offspring. Which explanation is most consistent with this new evidence?

options.0: The loci behave as effectively unlinked in this dataset; they may be on different chromosomes or far apart on one chromosome.
options.1: The estimated distance is 9.2 map units, assuming the recombinant classes are correctly identified and similarly viable.
options.2: The pattern supports M as the middle locus, with adjacent interval calculations needed for the map.
options.3: The loci must be on different chromosomes because recombination is near 50%.

otherActivityRecords.title: A fictional height-like trait has a broad range of measurements. Which model should be considered before assuming a simple 3:1 phenotype ratio?

options.0: Several contributing loci and environmental influences
options.1: A continuous range proves one completely dominant locus
options.2: Similarity among relatives rules out environmental effects
options.3: One allele fixes an unchangeable measurement in every environment

otherActivityRecords.title: A genetic variant is modestly associated with a complex trait in one studied population, but the association differs in another. What inference is supported?

options.0: The association needs validation in context and does not by itself prove a universal causal effect.
options.1: The first study proves that changing the variant will cause the same change everywhere.
options.2: The variant determines each individual’s exact trait value.
options.3: A result from one population transfers unchanged to every environment.

otherActivityRecords.title: Genetically matched plants grow to different mean heights under two light conditions. Which comparison best tests an environmental contribution?

options.0: Randomly assign matched plants to the two light treatments while holding other conditions constant
options.1: Compare unrelated plants from two sites that differ in soil, water and light
options.2: Compare genotype labels while recording no light treatment
options.3: Measure the tallest plant from each site and omit the remaining plants

otherActivityRecords.title: Relatives resemble each other for a trait influenced by many genes and their environment. What does this resemblance alone establish?

options.0: It is compatible with shared genetic and environmental influences but does not separate their contributions.
options.1: It proves a single dominant locus controls the trait.
options.2: It rules out an environmental contribution.
options.3: It guarantees identical measurements in every environment.

otherActivityRecords.title: What did Franklin’s X-ray diffraction work contribute?

options.0: Evidence constraining DNA’s helical regularity, dimensions, and molecular arrangement
options.1: A direct colour photograph of DNA bases
options.2: Proof that proteins never carry information
options.3: The complete genetic code

otherActivityRecords.title: A proposed DNA model puts sugar–phosphate backbones at the centre and unpaired bases facing outward. Which correction follows the usual double-helix model?

options.0: Place the backbones externally and complementary paired bases internally.
options.1: Keep the reversed positions because any two strands form the usual helix.
options.2: Replace all backbone bonds with the hydrogen bonds that connect paired bases.
options.3: Treat the central backbone as the normal product of simply separating the strands.

otherActivityRecords.title: A double-stranded DNA sample contains 28% adenine. What percentages of thymine and guanine follow from complementary base pairing?

options.0: 28% thymine and 22% guanine
options.1: 22% thymine and 28% guanine
options.2: 28% thymine and 44% guanine
options.3: 14% thymine and 36% guanine

otherActivityRecords.title: Two strands run in the same direction and bases pair without consistent complementarity. Which explanation is most consistent with this new evidence?

options.0: The model fails base-ratio and geometry constraints and offers a weak templating mechanism.
options.1: The problem is proved to be tightly crowded phosphate groups in the centre.
options.2: The model integrates chemical, Chargaff, and diffraction evidence and predicts template-based replication.
options.3: Having two strands makes the model correct regardless of direction or base pairing.

otherActivityRecords.title: Why are Okazaki fragments produced?

options.0: Antiparallel templates and 5-prime-to-3-prime synthesis require discontinuous lagging-strand synthesis
options.1: DNA polymerase synthesizes the lagging strand 3-prime to 5-prime
options.2: Helicase cuts chromosomes into genes
options.3: Ligase copies all DNA bases

otherActivityRecords.title: Templates are open, but no new DNA begins at expected initiation sites. Which is one possible mechanism to test, rather than a uniquely proven cause?

options.0: Without primers, DNA polymerase lacks a starting 3-prime end despite available template.
options.1: Synthesis occurred, but ligase-dependent sealing of fragment junctions is incomplete.
options.2: Reduced proofreading increases replication errors while not implying that every mismatch persists or changes phenotype.
options.3: Open DNA proves that polymerase can start without a primer.

otherActivityRecords.title: DNA grown in heavy nitrogen is transferred to light nitrogen. After one complete round of semiconservative replication, which DNA-molecule pattern is expected?

options.0: Each molecule has one old heavy strand and one new light strand
options.1: Half the molecules contain two heavy strands and half contain two light strands
options.2: Each molecule contains two new light strands
options.3: Each strand consists of alternating intact heavy and light nucleotides by a fixed pattern

otherActivityRecords.title: Lagging-strand DNA contains many completed fragments separated by backbone nicks. Which explanation is most consistent with this new evidence?

options.0: Synthesis occurred, but ligase-dependent sealing of fragment junctions is incomplete.
options.1: Without primers, DNA polymerase lacks a starting 3-prime end despite available template.
options.2: Reduced proofreading increases replication errors while not implying that every mismatch persists or changes phenotype.
options.3: The lagging fragments must have been synthesized 3′→5′ before joining.

otherActivityRecords.title: Which strand does RNA polymerase read?

options.0: The DNA template strand in the 3-prime-to-5-prime direction
options.1: The coding strand in the 5-prime-to-3-prime direction as a template
options.2: Both strands simultaneously for one transcript
options.3: The protein product

otherActivityRecords.title: The gene’s DNA sequence is present, but RNA polymerase occupancy and transcript abundance are low. Which explanation best connects this evidence to the lesson mechanism?

options.0: The evidence supports reduced transcription initiation rather than deletion of the gene.
options.1: Alternative splicing produced distinct mature transcripts from the same gene region.
options.2: Transcription increased, while translation efficiency or protein degradation may limit protein accumulation.
options.3: An intact DNA sequence must always be transcribed at a high rate.

otherActivityRecords.title: A model cell contains abundant mature mRNA for a gene but little stable protein from that gene. Which next measurements best distinguish two downstream explanations?

options.0: Measure translation rate and protein breakdown rate
options.1: Measure chromosome number and label the gene absent
options.2: Measure promoter activity only and assume mRNA cannot persist
options.3: Measure mRNA again and infer that each transcript makes exactly one protein

otherActivityRecords.title: Two mature RNAs are traced to the same gene region. Both retain exons 1 and 3, while only one retains exon 2. Which explanation fits this processing difference?

options.0: Alternative splicing produced distinct mature transcripts from the same gene region.
options.1: The evidence supports reduced transcription initiation rather than deletion of the gene.
options.2: Transcription increased, while translation efficiency or protein degradation may limit protein accumulation.
options.3: Different mature RNAs prove the cells inherited different chromosome sets.

otherActivityRecords.title: What directly recognizes an mRNA codon during elongation?

options.0: A complementary tRNA anticodon positioned by the ribosome
options.1: A DNA centromere
options.2: A stop amino acid
options.3: RNA polymerase

otherActivityRecords.title: A codon changes from GAA to GAG in the same reading frame; both specify glutamate. Which explanation best connects this evidence to the lesson mechanism?

options.0: The amino-acid sequence is unchanged, though RNA-level effects remain possible.
options.1: The immediate effect is a missense substitution; protein effect depends on position, chemistry, and structure.
options.2: Downstream codon grouping changes and a premature stop may appear, often producing a larger sequence consequence.
options.3: No change to the peptide proves that no RNA-level effect is possible.

otherActivityRecords.title: Use these code entries: GAA=Glu, GAG=Glu, GUA=Val. Coding DNA changes from 5′-GAA-3′ to 5′-GTA-3′ in the same reading frame. Which peptide-level prediction follows?

options.0: Glu changes to Val because the new RNA codon is GUA
options.1: Glu remains Glu because the new RNA codon is GAG
options.2: The codon becomes a stop because every substitution terminates translation
options.3: The reading frame shifts because one base was substituted

otherActivityRecords.title: A single-base substitution in a coding region changes a codon so that a different amino acid enters the polypeptide. Which immediate consequence follows?

options.0: The immediate effect is a missense substitution; protein effect depends on position, chemistry, and structure.
options.1: The amino-acid sequence is unchanged, though RNA-level effects remain possible.
options.2: Downstream codon grouping changes and a premature stop may appear, often producing a larger sequence consequence.
options.3: Every organism with the substitution must have the same final phenotype.

otherActivityRecords.title: Which statement about mutation is accurate?

options.0: A mutation is a DNA-sequence or chromosome change whose effect depends on location and context
options.1: Every mutation causes disease
options.2: Only environmental chemicals cause mutations
options.3: Somatic mutations are always inherited by offspring

otherActivityRecords.title: A base substitution occurs far from known splice and regulatory regions; RNA and protein measurements are unchanged. Which explanation best connects this evidence to the lesson mechanism?

options.0: The current evidence supports no detected functional effect under the tested conditions, not proof of no possible effect anywhere.
options.1: Converging recurrence and functional evidence supports a driver role in that tumour context.
options.2: The variant changes risk rather than guaranteeing disease, and counselling must address family information and uncertainty.
options.3: An unchanged assay proves no possible effect in any environment.

otherActivityRecords.title: A mutation appears in a skin-cell lineage but is not detected in the organism’s gametes. Which prediction follows most directly?

options.0: Descendants of that skin cell may inherit it through mitosis
options.1: Each offspring must inherit the mutation through fertilization
options.2: The mutation will be copied into every unrelated cell lineage
options.3: The mutation is automatically synonymous because it is somatic

otherActivityRecords.title: A variant recurs in tumours, activates a growth pathway in cells, and its inhibition reduces growth in matched models. Which explanation is most consistent with this new evidence?

options.0: Converging recurrence and functional evidence supports a possible contribution to growth in the studied tumour model.
options.1: The measurements demonstrate no detected functional difference.
options.2: The experiment establishes an individual’s inherited disease probability.
options.3: The same variant guarantees identical growth effects and treatment response in every tumour.

otherActivityRecords.title: What does DNA ligase do in recombinant-DNA construction?

options.0: It seals phosphodiester-bond breaks between compatible DNA ends
options.1: It recognizes every target gene
options.2: It copies RNA into protein
options.3: It selects transformed cells

otherActivityRecords.title: Colonies survive selection, but insert-specific PCR produces no product. Which explanation best connects this evidence to the lesson mechanism?

options.0: The result is consistent with a missing target insert or a failed insert assay; vector-only background is one possibility that requires controls.
options.1: Incorrect orientation or regulatory design can explain presence without expected transcription.
options.2: Translation, folding, modification, sequence error, or assay conditions remain possible after DNA and RNA verification.
options.3: Surviving selection proves the target insert is present and expressed.

otherActivityRecords.title: Colonies grow on antibiotic selection after receiving a plasmid intended to carry an inserted gene. Which next test most directly verifies that the desired insert has the intended sequence?

options.0: Sequence the insert and its junctions in a selected colony
options.1: Count colonies on the same selection plate again
options.2: Measure the antibiotic concentration without examining DNA
options.3: Infer the insert sequence from colony colour without a validated reporter

otherActivityRecords.title: Insert DNA is present, but transcript from the intended promoter is absent. Which explanation is most consistent with this new evidence?

options.0: Incorrect orientation or regulatory design can explain presence without expected transcription.
options.1: The selectable vector entered cells, but the target insert is absent; vector-only background is plausible.
options.2: Translation, folding, modification, sequence error, or assay conditions remain possible after DNA and RNA verification.
options.3: An insert must always be transcribed because its DNA is present.

otherActivityRecords.title: What does PCR do?

options.0: It amplifies selected DNA regions using primers and repeated cycles
options.1: It directly proves a person’s identity
options.2: It separates proteins by size
options.3: It translates DNA into amino acids

otherActivityRecords.title: A partial mixed sample includes alleles consistent with a person and with many possible relatives or unrelated contributors. Which explanation best connects this evidence to the lesson mechanism?

options.0: The partial match leaves multiple possible sources and needs further informative markers and quality checks.
options.1: The evidence already ranks one defined parent–child model over an unrelated model.
options.2: The result is a complete ancestry estimate.
options.3: One matching allele uniquely identifies the source of the whole sample.

otherActivityRecords.title: Two samples have matching band positions at one DNA marker. Which extension most improves discrimination between possible sources?

options.0: Compare additional informative independent markers with suitable controls
options.1: Repeat the same marker and report the matching bands as a whole-genome identity
options.2: Use band brightness alone as a unique inherited genotype
options.3: Discard samples from relatives because relatives cannot share marker alleles

otherActivityRecords.title: A child and tested adult share marker patterns more likely under one stated biological relationship than under an unrelated model. Which explanation is most consistent with this new evidence?

options.0: The result supports the tested relationship model probabilistically and depends on reference, mutation, and alternative-relative assumptions.
options.1: The evidence cannot identify one source without mixture modelling, population frequencies, quality evidence, and alternatives.
options.2: The estimate is model- and reference-dependent and should not be equated with culture, citizenship, Indigenous belonging, or complete family history.
options.3: The favored relationship is certain because all alternatives are impossible.

otherActivityRecords.title: What is the purpose of a negative control?

options.0: To reveal background signal or contamination when the target condition is absent
options.1: To guarantee the hypothesis is correct
options.2: To increase every measured value
options.3: To replace replication

otherActivityRecords.title: A PCR investigation finds products in every tube, including unexpected samples, but no blank control was run. Which explanation best connects this evidence to the lesson mechanism?

options.0: Contamination cannot be assessed; a negative control is needed before interpreting sample products.
options.1: The small deviation is compatible with sampling variation; a larger repeated sample and model check are needed.
options.2: The design supports auditable analysis, though model applicability and measurement uncertainty still require discussion.
options.3: A band in every sample proves that every sample has the uncontaminated target.

otherActivityRecords.title: For a predicted 1:2:1 genotype ratio, sample 1 has counts 3 AA, 5 Aa and 2 aa; sample 2 has 24 AA, 51 Aa and 25 aa. Which comparison is appropriate?

options.0: Compare frequencies with 0.25, 0.50 and 0.25, while considering the different sample sizes
options.1: Compare only the raw Aa counts, 5 and 51, to decide which cross has stronger dominance
options.2: Require every sample of ten to contain exactly 2.5 AA individuals
options.3: Treat the larger sample as proof that gametes always meet in a fixed sequence

otherActivityRecords.title: Six offspring are used to reject a 3:1 model because the observed ratio is 4:2. Which explanation is most consistent with this new evidence?

options.0: The small deviation is compatible with sampling variation; a larger repeated sample and model check are needed.
options.1: Contamination cannot be assessed; a negative control is needed before interpreting sample products.
options.2: The design supports auditable analysis, though model applicability and measurement uncertainty still require discussion.
options.3: The six offspring must exactly match 3:1 or segregation is false.

otherActivityRecords.title: A fictional crop-research project tests a genetic construct intended to support food production during drought. Use the pilot observations to distinguish the intended benefit, an unintended human consequence and a possible environmental consequence. Explain how further research could support a sustainable society, economy and environment. State an initial research priority. A grower then objects that trial costs make participation difficult. Revise the priority or justify retaining it with an adaptation. Name what to monitor before expansion, and explain why this pilot does not establish one cause or a final sustainability verdict.
A variant lies at a splice boundary, an exon is missing from mature RNA, and protein abundance is low. Which explanation best connects this evidence to the lesson mechanism?

options.0: The sequence, RNA, and protein evidence converge on disrupted splicing; cellular and organism outcomes still require evidence.
options.1: Chromosome-location and linkage evidence support an autosomal linked explanation over the initial pedigree shortcut.
options.2: Functional convergence supports a driver role while heterogeneity and clinical response remain uncertain.
options.3: The three observations prove a unique cause and every later phenotype.

otherActivityRecords.title: A transformed cell contains the verified insert but no detectable intended protein. Which investigation best separates an expression problem from a DNA-insert problem?

options.0: Measure gene-specific mRNA and protein under the intended expression conditions
options.1: Repeat the insert sequence and infer protein activity without measuring it
options.2: Compare antibiotic resistance only, because resistance proves every gene is expressed
options.3: Count DNA bands and interpret the count as the number of active proteins

otherActivityRecords.title: In a fictional model-organism investigation, a preliminary sketch labels two studied loci as X-linked. Verified physical evidence locates both on one autosome, and a phased test cross finds a large excess of parental combinations with low recombination. What should be revised?

options.0: Chromosome-location and linkage evidence support an autosomal linked explanation over the initial pedigree shortcut.
options.1: The sequence, RNA, and protein evidence converge on disrupted splicing; cellular and organism outcomes still require evidence.
options.2: Functional convergence supports a driver role while heterogeneity and clinical response remain uncertain.
options.3: All genes in the organism must have the same linkage pattern.

otherActivityRecords.title: A diploid cell has 8 chromosomes before DNA replication. Give chromosome, chromatid and set counts before and after replication, then distinguish homologues from sisters.

Construct a bar graph for the supplied illustrative counts: interphase 72, prophase 12, metaphase 6, anaphase 4, and telophase/cytokinesis 6. Choose labelled axes and a scale. Calculate mitotic index and explain what additional assumptions a phase-duration estimate requires.

Compare cytoplasmic division in a typical animal cell and a typical plant cell. Name the boundary-forming structure and direction of its development in each. Both images show two daughter nuclear regions, but only one shows a complete boundary between them. Explain why counting nuclei alone cannot establish the number of separate cells.
Track a cell with two homologous chromosome pairs through meiosis I and II. Name what separates and give chromosome numbers in each product.
Compare nondisjunction of one homologous pair in meiosis I with nondisjunction in only one meiosis II cell. Give the four product categories for the tracked chromosome.
Trace a plant life cycle from diploid sporophyte back to diploid sporophyte, labelling meiosis, mitosis and fertilization.
A fictional plant trait has alleles A and a with complete dominance. Compare AA, Aa and aa and explain why these symbols do not predict population frequency.
Explain how segregation connects an Aa parent's meiosis to an Aa × Aa Punnett square. Predict genotype and phenotype probabilities under complete dominance.

Cross Iᴬi with Iᴮi in the simplified ABO model. List gametes, offspring genotypes and phenotypes with probabilities; distinguish codominance from multiple alleles.
Under a fully penetrant autosomal recessive model, two unaffected parents have an affected child. Give parent genotypes and the carrier probability for another child known to be unaffected.

Write the complementary strand paired with 5′-ATGC-3′, then write that complementary sequence in its own 5′→3′ direction. Name one historical constraint supporting the model.
At a replication fork, explain why both new strands grow 5′→3′ even though one is made in fragments. Name the roles of primer, polymerase and ligase.
Given coding DNA 5′-ATGGAATTTTAA-3′, write aligned template DNA and the mRNA 5′→3′. Explain which strand RNA polymerase reads.

A negative PCR control has a band, and two sample bands are similar in size. Explain what can be concluded and identify a next check.

Compare mitosis and meiosis starting from an unreplicated diploid cell with 2n=6. Assume successful replication, division and cytoplasmic separation in a simplified model. Make seven labelled comparison rows: DNA replications, nuclear divisions, homologue pairing, structures separated, product number, product ploidy/chromosome count, and genetic similarity. Explain why “all products are guaranteed genetically identical” is too strong for either process.
Classify authentic cell images using chromosome alignment or separation. Explain how uncertain images should be recorded.
Compare a plant alternation-of-generations cycle with polyp/medusa phases in a cnidarian model.
For AaBb × aabb under independent assortment, construct gametes and the four expected offspring classes.
Cross a carrier mother XᴬXᵃ with an unaffected father XᴬY in a simple X-linked recessive model. Give risk among sons and among all children under equal sex probability.
A three-gene map has distances X–Y=8, Y–Z=5 and X–Z=13. Give order and one limit of pairwise mapping.
For template 3′-TAC CTT AAA ATT-5′, transcribe 5′→3′ and translate the indicated start frame.
Contrast a base substitution, a one-base insertion and a three-base insertion within a coding region.

These invented plant samples compare three different homologous regions. Within each panel, all sequences run 5′→3′ and positions are already aligned with equal coverage and no gaps. Count substitutions from that panel’s reference for X, Y and Z, and rank their similarity separately for each panel. For this fictional species, assume nuclear inheritance from both parents and mitochondrial/chloroplast inheritance through one parent. Explain a conditional relatedness inference, why the rankings can differ, and two checks or limits before making a whole-organism ancestry claim. Do not align different panels to each other.

Use one visible feature from the authentic images and keep it separate from the supplied synthetic counts. Calculate mitotic index and a conditional interphase-duration estimate using the 20-hour model. State a testable question and prediction about phase counts, then design a repeated comparison with consistent observation rules. A reviewer claims, “A large mitotic fraction proves rapid population growth.” Give an alternative explanation, revise that claim, and name a measurement that would distinguish the explanations.

Use the supplied Aa×Aa samples to state a testable question and prediction about sample size and genotype proportions. Compare observed and expected counts for one small and one large sample. Design repeated comparisons with parental genotypes, scoring and inheritance assumptions controlled. A reviewer claims, “Any departure from 1:2:1 disproves segregation.” Give another possible source of disagreement, revise the claim, and identify a check that would distinguish the explanations. Do not predict that every larger sample must be closer.

Use the supplied coding sequences and fragment measurements to ask a testable question and predict which method can distinguish a one-base change. Cite a sequence contrast and the complete fragment totals for reference and insertion models. Design a repeated comparison with suitable controls and consistent conditions. A reviewer claims, “Equal apparent gel-band size proves identical sequence.” Give an alternative explanation for similar bands, revise that claim and identify the more discriminating evidence. Keep the short coding excerpt separate from the measured larger fragments.

A model cell with 2n=4 completes normal meiosis I. One chromosome fails to separate its sisters in one of the two meiosis-II cells; the other cell divides normally. Give chromosome counts in all four products and compare the pattern with one meiosis-I nondisjunction event.

Both parents are AB/ab, with complete dominance at each locus. Change the model from independent assortment to complete linkage with no crossing over. Calculate P(aabb) and P(A_bb), and identify the offspring class that would disprove complete linkage in this cross.

Under full penetrance, two unaffected parents with an affected recessive child must both be Aa. Now allow some aa people to be unaffected. Does the usual 2/3 carrier probability for an unaffected sibling still follow? Explain what extra information is needed.

seminar.title: Review Seminar: match each claim to its evidence
introduction: Genetic evidence spans chromosomes, crosses, sequences, RNA, proteins and cell traits. Record each result with its method, sample, time, units and resolution. Put raw observations, calculated probabilities and inferred mechanisms in separate columns. One measurement cannot supply all the missing links between a DNA change and a phenotype.

Different mechanisms may fit the same result. Low protein can reflect low RNA, inefficient translation or rapid breakdown. A small pedigree can fit several inheritance models. Write the alternatives before choosing a test whose predicted results differ. Repeating a measurement that all alternatives predict will not necessarily distinguish them.

Keep denominators and references visible. A recombination fraction, a cross probability and an assay error rate answer different questions; do not multiply unrelated percentages into a personal prediction. A conclusion should identify what is supported, what remains open and what result would require revision.

Genetic information can affect relatives and communities. A responsible proposal identifies consent, privacy, access, cultural context and who controls data use, including relevant Indigenous data sovereignty. Use fictional observations here. Recommend an evidence or governance step without diagnosing or prescribing from a classroom model.

case.title: Three separate evidence sources
case.scope: Synthetic classroom models, not one person, family or continuous experiment. Their numbers must not be combined into an individual risk score.
rows: Chromosome model: 46 chromosomes arranged in the usual paired display.
One modelled metaphase cell; chromosome count and visible band pattern.
Small sequence changes and all other cell lineages.
Cross model: 24 AA, 51 Aa and 25 aa among 100 offspring of Aa × Aa.
Synthetic scored offspring; stated equal segregation and survival model.
Whether all alternative inheritance and scoring explanations are excluded.
Molecular models: coding GAA becomes GAG in the same frame; both samples have 400- and 600-base fragments.
Standard code: both GAA and GAG specify glutamate. Fragment lengths describe a separate larger sequence context.
RNA abundance, protein activity and complete identity of all DNA bases.

activities.prompt: State one supported conclusion from each source, naming its scale. For the cross, include the expected AA/Aa/aa counts; for the molecular model, separate size from sequence.
activities.modelResponse: Chromosomes: a typical count in one sampled cell. Cross: 24/51/25 is close to the 25/50/25 expectation. Molecules: GAA→GAG retains glutamate in this frame; matching 400/600-base fragments do not prove identical DNA.

activities.prompt: Evaluate the claim that these sources prove one person has unchanged protein function and zero inherited risk. Name an alternative explanation or unmeasured step and a test that would address it.
activities.modelResponse: The sources are separate and do not establish personal risk. An unchanged encoded amino acid does not measure RNA handling or protein function. Compare RNA and protein activity in matched models before linking the variant to a result.

activities.prompt: A peer notes that the sources are unrelated and a participant objects to secondary use of genetic data. Revise the claim and proposed next step, including who should control the proposed data use.
activities.modelResponse: Keep each source and denominator separate; the combined personal claim is unsupported. Test the molecular hypothesis in a matched fictional model. Define consent and participant or community control before any proposed secondary data use.
criteria: Consent and control over further use

seminar.title: Review Seminar: the North Marsh evidence board
introduction: An integrated case connects gene-pool change, abundance, life stages, habitat and interactions. Integration does not require one cause for every result. Record each observation with its source, units, timing and uncertainty before drawing arrows between them. A small population, a marker near Hardy–Weinberg expectations and declining recruitment answer different questions.

Population size and density use different denominators. Reduced habitat can partly offset the density effect of falling numbers, while the population still declines sharply. Mark–recapture adds another estimate with its own closure, mixing and detection assumptions. Agreement between two counts strengthens a size comparison without proving its cause.

A predator-first model predicts improvement when predator access is reduced. A habitat-first model predicts improvement when nesting conditions recover. A combined model predicts benefits from both, possibly with interaction. Compare a reference, habitat change alone, reduced predator access alone and both together, using repeated comparable plots and consistent recruitment measures. Observational categories alone do not supply random assignment.

Genetic management cannot be assumed to repair an ecological limitation. Moving organisms could add alleles, but habitat, disease transmission, compatibility and local adaptation also need evaluation. A marker near equilibrium does not show that every allele or adaptive trait is secure. Additional marker and demographic evidence is needed before a real intervention could be assessed.

A monitored classroom proposal names water level, vegetation, predator evidence, nest success, recruitment, adult survival and allele diversity as different indicators. Set a recruitment review after three years and an earlier stop rule for harm or unintended effects. Define the threshold before inspecting the outcome. No consultation, legal authorization or community endorsement is implied by this synthetic example.

For a worked decision rule, propose revising a pilot if recruitment per monitored plot has not improved relative to comparable reference plots after three years. Compare both initial differences and repeated measurements. Stop earlier for documented unintended harm under the agreed welfare protocol. This is an example of a revisable rule, not an ecological guarantee or permission to undertake field work.

case.title: North Marsh: supplied synthetic observations
case.scope: Fictional marsh-bird case retained from the original authored course. No real conservation decision, community view or field competence is claimed. Percentages have no supplied sample denominators or uncertainty intervals.
rows: Abundance
Adults declined from 420 to 210 over six years; a neighbouring population stayed near 600.
Different sites can differ in more than the proposed cause.
Density and survey
Density changed from 0.84 to 0.53 adults/hectare as occupied wetland contracted. At the later survey M=70,C=84,R=28.
Densities are supplied rounded values; mark–recapture requires closure, mixing, retained marks and comparable detection.
Genetics
Allelic richness declined; one neutral marker’s observed and expected genotype proportions were similar.
No actual genotype counts are supplied here; do not invent p,q or a formal goodness-of-fit result.
Timing
Juvenile recruitment fell before adult abundance; an introduced nest predator increased, while repeated low-water years left sparse vegetation.
Temporal order supports hypotheses without isolating their causes.
Nest categories
Success: dense/no predator signs 68%; dense/signs 39%; sparse/no signs 42%; sparse/signs 17%.
Signs are observations, not assigned treatments; denominators, repeated-site variation and other conditions are unprovided.

activities.prompt: Calculate the change in adult abundance as a percentage of the starting count and the mark–recapture estimate. Then explain why one marker near Hardy–Weinberg expectations does not rule out loss of diversity.
activities.modelResponse: Adults fell by 210/420 = 50%. Mark–recapture gives 70×84/28 = 210 under its assumptions. A fit at one marker is not proof of stable diversity across loci; allelic richness can decline while that comparison fits.

activities.prompt: Evaluate the claim that predator signs alone explain all nest failures. Use two supplied percentages and name a comparison that would help distinguish predator and habitat effects.
activities.modelResponse: Without predator signs, success is 68% in dense vegetation but 42% in sparse vegetation. Signs do not isolate cause. Compare repeated reference, habitat-only, exclusion-only and combined plots using matched recruitment measures.

activities.prompt: Revise a proposal to move birds immediately after a peer notes habitat loss and uncertain causes. State an evidence step and a monitoring rule, including an earlier reason to stop.
activities.modelResponse: Compare habitat and predator-access models with reference plots; moving birds alone may not restore recruitment. Review recruitment against references after three years; stop earlier for harm. Seek appropriate governance.

studyTasks.title: Identify the neuron parts and explain their jobs

choices.label: Run an unmyelinated axon
choices.resultTitle: Regeneration occurs along adjacent membrane
choices.observation: Each nearby membrane region must open channels and regenerate the action potential.
choices.reasoning: More membrane responds in sequence, so conduction is usually slower than in a similar myelinated axon.

choices.label: Run a myelinated axon
choices.resultTitle: Regeneration is concentrated at nodes
choices.observation: Current spreads beneath myelin and the action potential is regenerated mainly at nodes of Ranvier.
choices.reasoning: Myelin limits current loss, so the next node reaches threshold sooner without making each action potential larger.

choices.label: Model damaged myelin
choices.resultTitle: Current leaks before the next node
choices.observation: Less local current reaches the next node, so threshold may be delayed or not reached.
choices.reasoning: Loss of insulation can slow or interrupt conduction. The outcome depends on the location and extent of damage.

studyTasks.title: Label and read an action-potential graph
Explain the pump, channels, and forward signal

choices.label: Rest
choices.resultTitle: Resting membrane potential
choices.observation: The model is near −70 mV. Potassium leak and ion gradients help keep the inside negative relative to the outside.
choices.reasoning: The sodium-potassium pump maintains the gradients over time; it does not create the rapid spike by itself.

choices.label: Threshold
choices.resultTitle: Threshold starts the regenerative response
choices.observation: The membrane reaches about −55 mV and enough voltage-gated sodium channels open to sustain rapid depolarization.
choices.reasoning: A subthreshold change fades. Reaching threshold starts an all-or-none action potential.

choices.label: Rising phase
choices.resultTitle: The membrane depolarizes
choices.observation: Na+ moves into the axon down its electrochemical gradient, and voltage rises rapidly.
choices.reasoning: Positive charge entering makes the inside less negative and then positive.

choices.label: Peak
choices.resultTitle: Sodium entry stops increasing
choices.observation: Near +30 mV, sodium channels inactivate and delayed potassium channels are open.
choices.reasoning: The changing channel states turn the voltage away from the peak and begin repolarization.

evidence.label: Transition
evidence.value: Na+ channels inactivate; K+ channels are open

choices.label: Falling phase
choices.resultTitle: Potassium exit repolarizes the membrane
choices.observation: K+ leaves the axon while sodium channels remain inactivated, so voltage moves negative again.
choices.reasoning: The loss of positive charge from the inside produces the falling phase.

choices.label: Undershoot
choices.resultTitle: The membrane becomes briefly more negative
choices.observation: K+ channels close slowly, so potassium continues leaving after voltage passes its resting value.
choices.reasoning: Continued positive-charge loss produces hyperpolarization and contributes to the relative refractory period.

choices.label: Recovery
choices.resultTitle: Channel states return toward readiness
choices.observation: Potassium channels close and sodium channels recover from inactivation as voltage returns near rest.
choices.reasoning: Restored channel readiness allows another action potential. The maintained ion gradients support continued signalling.

records.prompt: How does changing one synaptic step alter the postsynaptic response?

choices.label: Block calcium entry
choices.resultTitle: Less neurotransmitter is released
choices.observation: The impulse arrives, but fewer vesicles fuse with the presynaptic membrane.
choices.reasoning: Calcium entry is the link between terminal depolarization and exocytosis.

choices.label: Block postsynaptic receptors
choices.resultTitle: Release is normal but the target response falls
choices.observation: Neurotransmitter enters the cleft and can be cleared normally, but it cannot activate the blocked receptors.
choices.reasoning: The disruption occurs after diffusion and before the target-cell electrical effect.

choices.label: Block cholinesterase
choices.resultTitle: Acetylcholine acts for longer
choices.observation: More acetylcholine remains available to bind receptors in the cleft.
choices.reasoning: Slower breakdown delays signal termination and may extend postsynaptic stimulation.
